1. A list for reckoning years

The fullest surviving list of ancient Olympic victors is preserved in the chronological work of Eusebius. It runs from the first Olympiad to the 249th, its main sequence generally identifying each Olympiad by the winner of the stadion race. This was the race over the full length of the track, Olympia's oldest event. There are occasional exceptions and notices of other events. What matters here is its basic way of locating Olympiads through their victors, rather than producing a modern table of performances in every event.

The list was not made for athletics. It was a calendar.

Ancient Greece had no common system for numbering years. Each city dated them by its own magistrates, and the months had different names. For an event involving two cities, each side had its own account of the year. The Olympic festival took place every four years, at a stable interval, and was recognized throughout the Greek world. The champion's name that appeared once every four years thus became a temporal coordinate available to everyone. To establish when something had happened, one could say that it occurred in the Olympiad when a particular man won the stadion.

The person generally credited with arranging the victors' names into a continuous catalogue is Hippias of Elis, around 400 BCE. The first champion was called Koroibos; later tradition dated his Olympiad to 776 BCE. From Hippias, the list passed through several generations of chronographers, then through Africanus, and finally into Eusebius. Eusebius's original no longer survives. What we use today comes through an Armenian translation and the Latin tradition.

One point must come first. When Hippias began compiling the list, nearly four hundred years had passed since its intended first Olympiad. He is unlikely to have invented the names out of nothing. Modern scholarship tends to think that he used local traditions in Elis, accounts of the sanctuary at Olympia, athletic treatises, and scattered notices of victors in local histories and victory odes. But before these materials were assembled into a continuous line, they were not a line. Today the entries for the earliest few dozen Olympiads are treated as usable but requiring assessment in layers, neither accepted wholesale nor discarded wholesale. There are three grounds for doubt: the long interval involved; the limited conditions for writing and preserving archives in early Greece; and inconsistencies within the tradition, including traces of later repairs. Pausanias's own accounts of when events were added expose these tensions.

Christesen has also pointed out something easily overlooked. Not every text mentioning a victor is a victor list. A victory ode says that its subject won at Olympia; a local history mentions an ancestor's championship. These are accounts of victories, but not a catalogue arranged by Olympiad. What distinguishes a catalogue is not that it records who won. It promises an entry for every Olympiad, with all entries arranged in the same way. The distance between scattered accounts and a continuous catalogue is a difference of form, not quantity. Hippias took precisely that step, turning the former into the latter. Once he had done so, victory accounts that had originally spoken separately acquired a common position, while losing their individual earlier shapes.

The construct's earliest product, in other words, was retrospective recognition. It arranged names scattered across four centuries into a line, and that line began to be used as time itself. The entire Greek world later used it to locate its history, although it had been made four hundred years after the beginning of the period to which it was applied.

The starting point of 776 BCE was calculated, too, rather than read from an archive. Given a continuous list, knowing the absolute date of any one Olympiad allows one to count backward to the first. That year was therefore a product of the list, not its foundation. Between the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the starting date prompted a substantial and sometimes heated dispute. Most people now use it as a traditional date rather than a verified historical milestone. A tool for dating other things had its own first year worked out by calculation.

What a construct produces depends on what it was made to do. This list was made to locate years, so all it needed was a champion's name for each Olympiad; the numbered Olympiad still distinguished the date when the same man won again. It did not need to know how long that person had taken to run. It did not even need him to be faster than the previous winner. For more than two thousand years afterward, people repeatedly searched the list for something it had never contained, then explained its absence as loss over the centuries. Things were indeed lost. This particular thing was not. It had never been produced.

2. The list needs only one name

At crown games such as Olympia, awards at the festival level went, in essence, only to the victor. There was no second prize, no third prize, no formal sequence of placings. Crowther puts the point clearly: only first place received the festival's award at the major Greek games. But he also cautions that it distorts matters to insist too absolutely that victory alone counted, since non-winning performances occasionally appear in literature and inscriptions.

The most famous example is Alcibiades. During the debate over the Sicilian expedition, he presented his credentials to the Athenians, mentioning that his entries at Olympia had taken first, second, and fourth in the chariot race. Thucydides recorded the speech. Herodotus, too, occasionally mentions someone finishing second.

Second place was therefore not unsayable. The important distinction lies elsewhere. Being spoken of and being entered in a register are different things. Alcibiades's second and fourth places entered Thucydides's text because they served his political argument that day. They entered no victor list because the list had no need of them. The same fact had a place in a narrative and no place in the institution.

This distinction will become very important later, so it is worth recognizing while it is still this simple. Narrative selects: what it records depends on what the teller needs at the time. The institution does not select in that way. It fills a predetermined form; everything that does not fit remains outside. Narrative seems more capacious because it can hold anything. But it promises to hold nothing, so what it contains depends entirely on contingency. Had Alcibiades not urged the Athenians to send an expedition on that occasion, those two placings would not be known. The institution seems less capacious, but it makes a promise. Within the small area it agrees to contain, something will not disappear merely because no one happens to mention it.

Here the construct is at its clearest. It does not suppress the runner-up, deny that he ran, or even forbid him from talking about it everywhere. It simply reserves no place for him. The remainder here is not a column that has been deleted, but a column that was never drawn. The whole subsequent history of athletics will return to this form: what a construct cannot clear away is often not what it has expelled, but what it never provided a place to receive.

The form of the rewards follows this arrangement. At the festival itself, the prize was a wild-olive crown and nothing more. The real remuneration came on returning to one's city: cash, public meals for life, front-row theatre seats, exemption from certain obligations. Xenophanes wrote a poem expressly complaining that a fast runner received far more than a wise man. Plutarch reports that Solon established rewards for Athenians: five hundred drachmas for an Olympic victor and one hundred for an Isthmian victor. The source of the report is clear, but Plutarch lived much later than Solon, and scholars dispute the reliability of the precise amounts. Some read it as a trustworthy preservation of ancient Athens's reward system, others as a later moralizing narrative about legislation.

We need not develop the opposition between amateur and professional here; it belongs to a later essay. For now, remember only the division of labour between rewards. What the festival gave had no price. A wild-olive crown was worth little as an object; its value lay in being unavailable for purchase. Everything the city gave had a price, one precise enough to be written into a decree. Something unpriceable and a sum that could be priced met successively in the same person. The link that converted one into the other was the name entered on the list.

Whatever the reliability of the amounts, the direction is clear. The city paid for a name, not a number. A name could be exchanged for money, a seat, or the way an entire family would be spoken of over generations. A number took no part in that exchange because there was no number.

3. Four tracks of different lengths

The tracks at the four great sanctuaries had different lengths. This is not an inference from texts but an archaeological measurement based on surviving starting lines, distance markers, and drainage channels beside the tracks. Olympia's track was approximately 192 metres long; Delphi's about 177.5 metres; Nemea's about 178 metres; and the later track at Isthmia about 181 metres. An archaeological interpretation also proposes a change at Isthmia from six hundred feet to 559 feet.

Olympia was nearly fifteen metres longer than Delphi. That is no small difference. If stadion races at these four sites had been timed, the times would have meant nothing as direct comparisons.

The Nemean material makes the point especially well. In both his excavation publications and on-site explanations, Miller stresses that the track measured six hundred local feet, or about 178 metres. Yet the measured spacing of the markers placed every hundred feet is irregular. Miller therefore states directly that the ancient arrangement of those markers was not intended to produce precise performances in the modern sense.

The force of this evidence lies in its material existence. Someone says that ancient texts record no performances; someone else replies that the texts were lost. But the track is there, and the spacing of the markers can be measured. We cannot simply read these irregularly spaced markers as the equal, precise intervals of a modern scale. Unequally spaced markers can, of course, serve measurement when their distances are known; the question is what these particular markers actually did. They were not set at uniform intervals despite belonging to an age whose stoneworking could have achieved them. At least that prevents us from assigning them the purpose of a modern scale without further examination. The evidence supports a narrower point: producing exact performances for comparison across venues was not their primary purpose. It does not show that the ancients never measured anything.

We should pause here, because this is where an erroneous judgment comes most easily. Non-standard track lengths were not a defect in this construct. A defect is a failure relative to a purpose. Comparison across sanctuaries was never its purpose, so the four different track lengths posed no problem for anyone at the time. No one complained because no one needed them to be equal.

One feature makes the point even firmer. The same athlete might compete at several sanctuaries within one year. The four great festivals followed staggered cycles, and anyone aspiring to win the entire circuit had to visit all four. The same pair of legs, then, ran four tracks of different lengths in the same season. If anyone had cared about comparability, that athlete would have been the first to discover the problem, because the difference bore directly on his own body. Yet no surviving account shows anyone proposing a conversion or complaining that running at Delphi was easier than running at Olympia. What he wanted was four crowns. Four crowns did not require equal lengths.

We can press the question further. If the lengths differed, was winning on a long track harder than winning on a short one? Today the question seems natural. At the time it could not have been asked in this form, because it assumes that two competitions can be placed on a single scale of difficulty. The contemporary scale was the opposition. Winning at Olympia was difficult because the strongest competitors gathered there, not because its track was the longest. In weighing a victory, the construct considered whom it defeated, not how many metres it covered.

When we read these figures today, our instinct is to convert them: if all distances were standardized to 192 metres, what would a Delphic performance become? That instinct comes from a later construct, not from the event itself. To treat a subsequently created need as though it had always existed, then accuse the ancients of failing to satisfy it, is one of the commonest misreadings of ancient institutions. It will mislead us all the way into the nineteenth century.

One incidental point also needs clarification. Track length was reckoned in local feet, and feet differed between places. Six hundred feet was therefore the same number at the four sanctuaries; what differed was the foot. People used the same number, measured different lengths, and saw no contradiction. The number belonged to the ritual; the length belonged to the site. Standardizing the number without standardizing the actual length was entirely coherent in a world with no intention of comparing across venues. The later construct does precisely the reverse: it standardizes actual length and abandons the ritual number. Four hundred metres is four hundred metres; a metre is a metre. What a metre is has been decided elsewhere, independently of the stadium. What separates the two arrangements is purpose, not precision.

4. Measurement did occur, and we still cannot settle it

Antiquity was not entirely without numbers. A few survive, and all are startling.

An epigrammatic tradition credits Phayllos of Croton with a jump of fifty-five feet and a discus throw of ninety-five feet. The text comes down through later commentaries and the Suda; Harris devoted a study to the poem in 1960. Chionis of Sparta also has a recorded measurement, but its number is unstable. The Eusebian tradition that can be checked today gives twenty-two feet. Other scholarly traditions, drawing on Africanus or textual emendation, argue for fifty-two. Strictly handled, fifty-two feet must be marked as a disputed emendation, not presented as an uncontested value.

Fifty-five feet converts to roughly sixteen metres. The modern long-jump world record is 8.95 metres. Either the ancient number refers to a different activity, or it is unreliable.

Jumping did involve equipment. Athletes held a pair of jumping weights. Pausanias describes their form as semicircular but somewhat elliptical, with openings for the fingers. Philostratus says that the weights were an invention of pentathletes, and mentions rules permitting flute music to assist their rhythm. Modern biomechanical experiments support the proposition that jumping weights can help: suitable weights can produce gains measured in centimetres. Centimetres. That is nowhere near a doubling to sixteen metres.

The flute is worth noticing, too. Philostratus says the rules allowed flute music to support rhythm. Jumping was thus an accompanied event. An accompanied event and a stopwatch-timed event attend to different things. Accompaniment serves the execution and spectacle of movement; a stopwatch serves the comparability of results. The rules of the time were willing to legislate for the former, suggesting where the event's perceived importance lay.

Four explanations therefore remain side by side, with none able to displace the others. First, multiple jumps: a research group at Ghent and many subsequent scholars propose that the event may have consisted of five consecutive standing jumps. Experiments can indeed produce totals exceeding fifteen metres. Second, a different competitive format: other scholars argue that this was not a single long jump in the modern sense, and may have involved a prescribed approach area and a different method of measurement. Third, textual corruption, particularly in Chionis's case: numbers could certainly have changed during copying. Fourth, rhetorical exaggeration. Discussing the poem about Phayllos, Harris explicitly included literary embellishment and satirical exaggeration among the possible explanations, since epigram allows them.

These numbers are still disputed precisely because there was no ledger against which to check them. They came from a poem, not an archive. A poem may exaggerate, be misreported, or gain or lose a character in transmission. A ledger cannot work that way. For a number to become checkable, someone merely writing it down is insufficient. An institution must promise that it will be recorded, and that a second and a third number will be recorded in the same way.

This is the point requiring the greatest care in this essay. Isolated numerical values do not establish that a system for routinely checking performances already existed. To check Phayllos's jump, we would need the marks of his contemporaries at the same festival, results from the same event in adjacent Olympiads, and a distribution against which to judge its implausibility. The surviving material supplies none of these references. That does not exclude every measurement whose record has been lost, but it means that this number alone cannot reconstruct a verifiable record system. It stands alone in a poem: twenty-five centuries, four readings.

Put differently, a number's reliability never comes from itself alone. It comes from the other numbers around it. If someone today announces a performance far beyond the world record, judging its authenticity need not require returning to the scene. We can examine its position in the distribution, the other competitors' results, the athlete's previous performance curve, and the wind and venue on the day. Together those references form a net. A number acquires weight when it lands in that net. The number attached to Phayllos has no net. There is empty space beneath it, so it can be neither verified nor falsified, only interpreted. Interpretation admits many possibilities; that is why the four explanations still stand together.

The modern reader's first response is usually to ask what the distance really was. That question already assumes the number can be determined. A more accurate approach recognizes that a number not intended to be checked and one intended to be checked are not the same kind of thing at all, even if they look identical on the page.

5. A highly developed construct, measuring something other than performance

Olympia's judges were called the Hellanodikai, the judges of the Greeks. Pausanias explicitly records repeated changes in their number as the system changed. At first, Iphitos supposedly acted alone. From the fiftieth Olympiad there were two, selected by lot. At the ninety-fifth their number rose to nine, and later to ten. There were twelve at the 103rd, then eight at the 104th after the number of tribes was reduced. At the 108th it returned to ten and remained there.

This sequence tells us a good deal on its own. The number of judges followed the number of tribes in Elis: when tribes were added or removed, judges were added or removed. An administrative reorganization outside the stadium determined how many people made decisions inside it. The construct's internal structure was determined by an external structure. In the festival's own account, this posed no problem, because it had never claimed that the number of judges arose from athletic considerations.

Their selection and duties also have direct textual attestation. Chosen from among the people of Elis, they had to spend ten consecutive months in the judges' residence there, receiving instruction from the guardians of the laws. On competition day they arrived before dawn to assign runners to heats; at midday they supervised the pentathlon and the heavy events. They were both judges and administrators of the festival.

Then there were the oaths. Pausanias records that the athlete, his father and brothers, and his trainer had to swear before the statue of Zeus of Oaths that he had completed the prescribed ten months of training and would not cheat at the games.

The range of people swearing deserves attention. Only one person competed, but his father, brothers, and trainer swore as well. The construct distributed responsibility among a circle of non-competitors. The reason is not hard to infer: only the people around an athlete knew whether he had really trained for ten months. The festival could not inspect those months, so it required those who knew to stake themselves alongside him. This is a characteristic response. When a construct cannot directly observe something, it finds an observable substitute and requires that substitute to vouch for the original.

There were punishments, too: corporal punishment, fines, and disqualification. Specialist whip-bearers administered flogging. Lichas was whipped on the spot for breaking the rules by tying a victory ribbon around his own charioteer. The bribery case involving Eupolos is documented in detail. Most interesting of all was the use made of fines. They paid for statues of Zeus placed along the approach to the stadium, with the offenders' names and warnings inscribed on the bases. That row of stone bases still stands at Olympia today.

Taken together, these are hardly the features of a crude construct: ten months of training; pre-competition oaths; judge numbers adjusted to the tribes; drawing lots; assigning heats; whippings; fines; and a row of warnings cast with those fines and placed where everyone had to pass. This apparatus was no less elaborate than the disciplinary provisions of a modern competition. Some parts were harsher still.

Later generations often explain the lack of ancient athletic numbers by saying that development had not yet reached that stage. This evidence does not support that explanation. Developed and undeveloped are earlier and later positions on one axis. Here there are two axes. The construct invested all its precision along another axis: it wanted to ensure that a victory was clean, not determine the magnitude of a performance. Its vigilance against fraud was extremely high; its interest in magnitude approached zero.

Nor is there any necessary connection between those two things. A festival can rigorously police cheating and time performances precisely; today's competitions do both. It can also do only the first, as the ancient games did. Treating them as two aspects of the same progress is a later habit. Integrity and magnitude are independent questions. A construct can answer only one, and answer it very well.

The point can be pushed further. Measuring how fast someone runs and judging whether someone has won lawfully are different jobs, requiring different apparatuses. The former needs standardized rulers and clocks; the latter needs supervised oaths, oversight, investigation, and punishment. Antiquity devoted its resources to the latter and developed it thoroughly. Precision is therefore not something that accumulates along a single line. It always grows in a particular direction, determined by what the construct intends to produce.

The Zeus statues cast from fines are the most solid instance in this section. Fines were intended to remove cheating from the festival. The method of removal was to cast the cheats' names in bronze and place them on the route every entrant had to take. What had been expelled remained on the spot as a warning. More than that: the bases remain today, while the great majority of victors' statues have vanished. What the construct sought to eliminate outlived what it sought to honour.

6. Who gets entered?

Kyniska won the four-horse chariot race at Olympia twice, in 396 and 392 BCE. Pausanias records that she erected a statue at Olympia. Its inscription survives and declares her the only woman in all Greece to have won that crown. This is securely established, not disputed.

She did not drive the chariot. Victory in chariot racing was credited to the owner of the horses, not the driver.

The driver did everything. He is absent from the list. His name was not recorded; we do not know his city or whether he was free or enslaved.

The construct had not failed to notice him. Chariot-racing rules necessarily governed drivers: starts, fouls, crashes. Drivers bore the consequences, and the whip struck their bodies. He therefore existed in the rules but not in the list. A person can be fully governed by an institution while remaining entirely unrecorded by it. Jurisdiction and recording are different acts. The first requires his presence; the second requires his being named. This construct needed him only where it needed him present. Its rule was perfectly explicit and unambiguously enforced: victory belonged to the horse-owner.

Eligibility was less rigid than popular accounts suggest, too. Herodotus reports that Alexander I of Macedon first had to prove that he was Greek before competing. He was admitted after presenting a genealogical argument connecting him with Argos. Traditional textbooks turn this into a restriction to free Greek males. Remijsen, however, has proposed a substantial revision: the notion of a formal rule excluding non-Greeks from the Panhellenic games is, in large part, a nineteenth-century nationalist reconstruction. The evidence reads more like negotiations over who counted as Greek in particular situations than a stable, universally applicable law. This is a dispute of interpretation, not an established rule. Both readings must remain visible here.

The position of enslaved people and non-citizens is more obscure. The exclusion of enslaved people can be treated as a highly probable consensus, but direct, explicit evidence is thinner than popular writing implies. The proposition that an entrant had to be a citizen of a particular polis requires even greater caution. Royalty, colonial populations, elites who moved across regions, and the chariot system crediting horse-owners all suggest practices more flexible than modern nationality law.

For women there was another construct. The Heraean games certainly existed. They offered footraces for girls, divided by age: the youngest ran first, then the middle group, then the oldest. Their course was slightly shorter than the men's stadion. This was a separate festival, not an expansion of the same construct.

The distinction will recur throughout the history of athletics, so it should be marked now. When a construct encounters people it cannot accommodate, it has two options: push its own boundary outward to include them, or establish another construct alongside it. The second may also look like acceptance, but accomplishes two things at once. It gives those people somewhere to go while ensuring that the original construct need not change a word. The Heraean and Olympic festivals were separate events, held on different days, directed by different people, over different distances. They never needed a common list. As for the prohibition on married women watching, Pausanias reports an Elean law requiring women found at Olympia on forbidden days to be thrown from Mount Typaion. The story of Kallipateira rests on this prohibition. Modern doubts concern not the existence of the prohibition tradition, but its scope and the frequency of enforcement. It targeted married women rather than all females; priestesses and certain functional roles may have been exempt. The extreme penalty of being thrown from a cliff looks more like a normative threat, with insufficient evidence of actual executions. The cautious conclusion is that the tradition has a historical basis, but enforcement may have been considerably more flexible than the literal law suggests.

Everyone in this section stands, in one way or another, beside the edge of the list. Kyniska entered it; the man who drove for her did not. Alexander entered by virtue of a genealogy rather than a race. The girls at the Heraean games entered another list. Those targeted by the prohibition had even their eligibility to watch adjudicated.

Before measuring, the construct draws a line around who may be measured. That line produces no number, but determines the pool from which every subsequent number will emerge. This layer has never disappeared from the history of athletics. Only the grounds of the line change: from ancestry to nationality, from sex to hormone levels, from the body to equipment. Whatever the grounds, the line remains.

7. The ancients did compare, just not through numbers

Circuit victor was a title. It identified someone who had won at all four great festivals. The title was cumulative. Rather than fixing the speed of one performance in a ledger, it accumulated successive conquests at four sanctuaries into a recognizable identity.

It did perform part of the work of comparison. One could ask who had completed the circuit, who had done so earlier, and who had done so more than once. Related comparisons concerned total crowns, total family victories, and the surpassing of earlier or later competitors' crown counts. Pausanias includes comparisons of this kind between families.

There is another structural difference. Accumulated honours need no central institution to keep them. They grow on inscriptions, statue bases, victory odes, and the word placed before someone's name when he is introduced. Anyone may repeat them; anyone may carve them. Numerical records cannot work this way. They need a place of ratification, or several contradictory best marks will coexist for the same event. The cumulative system distributes custody among everyone; the numerical system must concentrate certification in one place. Cumulative honours can, of course, be disputed, but the dispute concerns entitlement to the honour, not whether a number counts.

To say that antiquity had no concept of records is therefore too sweeping. The ancients were interested in comparison and made something specifically to perform it. That something was a sequence of honours rather than a number. More precisely, antiquity lacked a unified numerical-record system permitting direct comparison across venues and eras. This is not a verbal nicety. It determines how the whole construct operates.

The cumulative system has a property that the numerical system lacks, and it deserves separate attention. No later athlete can break someone's title of circuit victor. It can only be matched or exceeded in frequency. It does not become invalid; no one crosses it out on some later afternoon. It is a biography, not a line.

A numerical record is different. Its mode of existence is to await erasure. Every establishment of a record simultaneously announces that prospect. Here the two constructs diverge, and nearly all the difficulties in the rest of this series grow along the numerical branch. The cumulative system need not manage provisionality because it produces none. It produces a sequence that only grows, never shrinks. Once an item enters, it remains forever.

The cost lies in the same place. The cumulative system cannot answer any question about speed. It can tell you who was the best athlete of an age, but not whether he was faster or slower than someone from another age. Between two circuit victors separated by three hundred years, no quantity can be set side by side. A sequence of honours can be extended, but cannot be converted across generations.

It has a less obvious cost, too. The cumulative system rewards persistence and completeness, not an extreme reached on a particular day. Someone who ran faster than anyone had ever run on one afternoon, but won nothing elsewhere, would have no place in this system. His afternoon would leave no trace. A numerical system would retrieve him; the cumulative system would not. Conversely, someone who won every time but struggled to win each time would rank at the top in a cumulative system and might count for nothing in a numerical one. The two constructs select different people and miss different people.

That is this construct's boundary. It is not worse than its successor. It solves another problem, and solves that problem thoroughly. The people it leaves as remainders are not the same people left by the numerical system.

8. Later generations needed it to have one

We cannot settle how the ancient games ended.

The familiar account says that Theodosius I banned them in 393 CE. Modern scholarship generally finds this too crude: no fully preserved edict explicitly names and abolishes the Olympic festival. More recent research tends to understand the end as a process stretching from the late fourth into the fifth century, involving anti-pagan legislation, the decline of sacrificial functions, local finances, and environmental disasters. Among alternative dates, 426 is common, associated with more thorough anti-pagan repression and destruction of sanctuaries. Other scholars prefer no single terminal year, describing the festival as becoming wholly unsustainable only as late as the mid-fifth century.

A list used to locate years for the whole Greek world has no year for its own ending. The instrument of chronology has no chronology of its own. This is not a coincidence; it is the same matter as everything preceding it in this essay. From beginning to end, the construct produced names. The death of an institution does not enter any list under someone's name. It had prepared no entry for its own conclusion.

One further point is possible. Part of the reason the end cannot be fixed is that the festival was not something that could be switched off in a single act. It was sacrifice, a market, an occasion for arbitration, a place where cities exchanged news. Athletics was only one layer. A decree could prohibit sacrifice, but not prevent people from going to the same place at the same time. Its disappearance was therefore layered. Each layer had its own time, and those times did not coincide. Something built from many layers will not have a tidy date of death.

Fifteen hundred years later it was made again, and those who remade it needed it to have been something else.

The revival of 1896 packaged several things with no ancient basis as a return to the ancient spirit. Amateurism was one. Ancient athletics had belonged from the outset to a system of rewards, patronage, fame, and civic compensation. Pure competition without material return was a projection of nineteenth-century aristocratic and gentlemanly sporting ethics onto antiquity. The marathon was another. Ancient Olympia had no such event; Bréal and Coubertin introduced it in 1896. An ideology centred on international peace and universal brotherhood was another, a product of late nineteenth-century internationalism and nation-state politics. The priority of participation was another. Ancient competitive culture emphasized victory, glory, and shame, not participation.

There was one more: a unified conception of records.

The important thing is not to catch the revivalists making mistakes. Many were competent classicists, and these constructions were made openly at the time, not concealed. The important question is why they needed those things to have existed.

A newly established institution asks the whole world to measure the same activity with the same ruler, and asks everyone to accept that its results are valid across national borders and historical periods. Such an institution needs an origin that establishes that its ruler was not invented yesterday. A newly invented ruler can be challenged; a ruler with more than a thousand years behind it is harder to question. Antiquity was therefore requisitioned. But antiquity had no ruler, only a long sequence of names. Names could not validate a ruler. So the ruler was supplied afterward, inserted into the past.

It was supplied in very concrete form. The amateur principle did not remain a slogan. It became eligibility screening, grounds for annulled placings, and the actual fate of athletes over the decades that followed. Once a mistaken judgment about antiquity enters a constitution, it ceases to be merely a judgment. It becomes an enforceable rule. Whether or not it has an ancient basis makes no difference to the person it disqualifies. This is a situation we will encounter repeatedly: a construct's source of legitimacy can be fictional without diminishing its practical force in the slightest.

From here on, the remaining essays in this series address one matter: the ruler added retrospectively was taken seriously, and really was built. It began to measure, with increasing precision. With every increment of precision, what could not fit its measurements emerged in a clearer shape.

The ancient festival operated for more than a thousand years and left a long list of names. None of the things we might expect to follow those names survives. They were never produced, rather than lost. The same applies to everything at the list's edge: the man who drove for Kyniska; Alcibiades's two unregistered placings; the actual distance of Phayllos's jump; the times run between Nemea's unevenly spaced markers. These were not erased. The construct had no column for them.

One last qualification is necessary. They are not all grievances. The charioteer may not have felt mistreated. He lived in a world in which chariot victories belonged to horse-owners; those were the rules he knew. A remainder is not synonymous with a victim. It is the part that the construct's accounts do not accommodate. What the people in that part thought of themselves is unknown to the construct, and inaccessible to us today. To make every person outside the list into a wronged innocent would be to let a later construct speak for them, precisely what this essay has tried to avoid.

The later construct added that column. Only then did it discover that one column was not enough.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

This list was made to locate years, so all it needed was a champion's name for each Olympiad; the numbered Olympiad still distinguished the date when the same man won again. For more than two thousand years afterward, people repeatedly searched the list for something it had never contained, then explained its absence as loss over the centuries. Things were indeed lost. This particular thing was not. It had never been produced.

edits.before:
When the newspaper became a ledger

Modern athletics did not discover records waiting in nature. It assembled the conditions under which a performance could count beyond the day on which it happened. Nineteenth-century sporting papers became early registries because they printed results repeatedly, compared meetings, corrected reports, and made claims visible to a dispersed public.

Publication alone was insufficient. A reported mark had to survive doubt. Was the course the right length? Who held the watch? Was the implement legal? Had the athlete received prohibited payment? The record emerged through repeated acts of refusal as much as acceptance. Institutions learned what evidence they required by encountering performances they did not trust.

Three watches and a vote

Hand timing shows the structure in miniature. A race is singular, but several timekeepers watch it separately. Rules eventually specified how their readings should be combined: agreement could settle the result, while disagreement required a prescribed choice rather than an improvised average. The official time was therefore not simply what one watch displayed. It was the output of a procedure governing several fallible observations.

Field events required equivalent scaffolding. Take-off lines, circles, sectors, implement dimensions, level measurement, and calibrated tapes made distance portable. A twelve-inch board and an eighteen-inch one did not merely produce slightly different contests; they produced results that could not inhabit the same book without a rule deciding which geometry defined the event.

The modern record is thus institutional before it is numerical. Precision belongs not only to instruments but to roles: who may observe, which reading prevails, where measurement begins, and what documentation follows the mark.

A federation builds a past

When an international federation takes responsibility for records, it performs three tasks. It states the events and conditions it will recognize; it decides what evidence future claims must supply; and it constructs an initial table from performances achieved before the rules were fully consolidated.

That third task is easily overlooked. The first official list necessarily reaches backward. Earlier competitions did not stage themselves for a later federation, yet selected performances are retrospectively admitted as ancestors of the present ledger. The record book presents a smooth chronology only because discontinuous newspapers, club minutes, and national lists have been converted into a common institutional form.

The operation resembles the ancient victor list but changes its object. Hippias' catalogue turned scattered names into a calendar. The modern record table turns scattered measurements into a progression. Both create continuity after the fact, and both later appear to have merely documented continuity that was already there.

What recognition leaves out

An official application can demand place, date, officials, equipment, course, wind, and timing. It cannot contain everything that made the performance possible. Training knowledge, nutrition, track composition, altitude, travel, weather, and the athlete's changing body exceed the form. The record construct does not deny these causes. It selects the subset that can be standardized and audited.

That selection gives the number its force. A mark becomes more than a result when other institutions agree to inherit it, compare against it, and replace it only through the same kind of evidence. The famous progression line is therefore not nature's ranking of human bodies. It is the history of performances that passed a particular gateway.

The book prefers addition

Once a performance enters the ledger, removal is difficult. The evidence for admission was gathered at the event; evidence for deletion may emerge decades later, after witnesses and documents have dispersed. Administratively, adding a new record is routine. Declaring an old one never to have counted threatens every dependent table and story.

This asymmetry will recur throughout the series. The record system presents itself as a neutral memory, yet it has a direction: it is designed to accumulate. Its authority comes from requiring proof at entry. Precisely because entry was once certified, later subtraction demands an exceptional burden.

The invention of the record was therefore not the invention of the stopwatch. It was the invention of a durable chain of custody linking a performance to a public number. The device measures seconds; the construct decides which seconds can become history.

1. A newspaper becomes a register

In 1868 a handbook called Modern Athletics, by Wilkinson, appeared in Britain. It included tables listing the best performances then known in various events. In the preface, Wilkinson explained where the numbers came from.

Some authority, he said, had to be adopted as the standard. He had chosen Bell's Life in London because it was the oldest reliable chronicler of professional pedestrianism.

We should pause over that sentence. It predates every governing body for athletics. There were no world records, no international organization, not even a national amateur athletic association. Yet there were already numbers described as the best performances on record, and their register was a commercial newspaper.

The newspaper had not been founded for sport. It served an earlier, more practical need. Nineteenth-century Britain had an entire professional running industry. People bet on races, and bets required verifiable results. How far a race had been run, how long it had taken, and who had timed it had to be discoverable somewhere, or wagers could not be settled. The newspaper was that place. It published results each week and, as the weeks accumulated, became an archive.

There is a subtle displacement here. A newspaper recorded a race result because readers wanted to know it. It retained years of results in bound volumes because that was how newspapers were kept, not because someone intended to establish an archive. The archive was a by-product. When Wilkinson needed a source, this by-product happened to be the only one large enough and continuous enough. When a construct chooses its ledger, it often chooses not the one prepared for it, but the one that happens still to exist.

Something thus happened that would recur throughout the later history of athletics. Before a construct acquired a body, it acquired a ledger. And that ledger belonged to someone else, serving someone else's purpose.

There is a more important implication in Wilkinson's sentence. He said that some authority had to be chosen. The necessity did not refer to how reliable Bell's Life was. It meant that without choosing, one could not begin. Every table of performances needs a source. The table cannot grant the source its qualifications; these have to come from outside. He selected the thing at hand that looked most like an archive.

There is something uncomfortable about this act. What is selected acquires authority because it has been selected, while the reason for selecting it is that it previously appeared most authoritative. There is no external intervention that can break this loop. At the bottom of every system demanding verification lies an act of designation of this kind, with no further layer beneath it against which to check the designation itself.

The same act continued. After the international federation was established, it had to decide which older performances could enter its first table, and again needed sources from outside. Later still, every dispute over a record's validity would eventually come down to some recording apparatus designated trustworthy. Why that apparatus was trustworthy could never be answered by the apparatus itself.

An incidental caution: looking back today, it is tempting to trace the origin of records to gambling, but that goes beyond the evidence. We can establish that money and verification were tightly intertwined at the beginning. We cannot establish that gambling alone created the institution. A layered account fits the evidence better: first came the verification needs of commerce and the press; clubs supplied rules in the middle; and the governance needs of international competition arrived last. It was this last layer that turned the record into a worldwide institution.

2. Rejection precedes acceptance

The same 1868 handbook contains another passage. Wilkinson complains that astonishing performances are constantly reported from various places, only to collapse on examination: the course was downhill, the distance too short, the timekeeper inexperienced, or the wind favourable.

Not a word mentions a rule, because there was no record rule at the time. Yet the grounds for rejection were already assembled: gradient, distance, a timekeeper's competence, wind. Most of the principal tests through which World Athletics puts a record today can be found here in embryonic form. They emerged not as legislation, but as reasons for dismissing particular reports.

This is a common way for a construct to be born. Its boundaries are not drawn first and then enforced. They are discovered through repeated refusals. People first know what does not count; much later they write down what does. The written version is largely a compilation of the earlier reasons for rejection.

This sequence explains something else. Rules often read as affirmative descriptions of what qualifies. Their actual formation runs in the opposite direction: behind each stands a particular performance once rejected. The finer the provisions, the more earlier disputes there have been. Read only the clauses in a history of rules and you see an increasingly complete system. Ask what forced each clause into existence and you see a succession of problems.

One point needs clarification lest this become a story of progress. Grounds for rejection could be discovered only because someone cared whether the number was right. The first people to care were those who depended on it to settle accounts. From the outset, the strictness of verification followed practical stakes, not a desire for truth. This is no criticism of the people involved. It merely identifies where the habit grew.

A detail gives this layer a more concrete form. In his chapter on organizing meetings, Wilkinson recommends a noticeboard at the ground, positioned so that spectators and members of the press can see it. It should display competitors, placings, times, and measured distances.

This was not a plan for publicity after the event. It built recordability directly into the physical arrangement of the competition. While being staged, a race was already preparing for its future appearance on paper. The number had to be available for copying; the copyist had to see it clearly; it would then enter a newspaper, which someone would later consult as an archive. That chain was complete in 1868. It simply had no institution attached to it yet.

Notice what appeared on the board: competitors, placings, times, measured distances. Place and time were written side by side, whereas for many preceding years place had been the only thing needing announcement. Putting time on the same footing as place declared that the race produced two products: one belonging to victory on the day, the other to comparisons on paper. The two have coexisted ever since, and do not always point to the same person.

The venue itself was being transformed in the same direction. Wilkinson still allowed races on grass, provided the course was properly marked. But he preferred purpose-built tracks, because performances were faster and measurement more accurate.

The two reasons deserve consideration together. Faster and more accurate appeared in the same recommendation. They had never been separated. A surface that allowed faster running was also one that could be measured more precisely, and the construct's preference for both was coupled from the start. All the later arguments about synthetic tracks, running shoes, and equipment that improves performances can be traced to this moment when the two remained undivided.

3. Three watches vote

In 1887 Shearman published Athletics and Football, reproducing the Amateur Athletic Association's current competition rules.

Those general rules required one timekeeper. Singular.

But Shearman's description of actual championship practice said something different. Championships used three timekeepers. He supplied the reason: in an age of continual record-breaking, there must be no doubt about the time. If all three watches differed, the middle reading was taken. If one differed from the other two, the majority prevailed.

This is the most important passage in the essay.

Three people watch the same person cover the same distance and obtain three numbers. All three are genuine observations. No one is cheating; no watch has broken.

To see the issue clearly, begin with an apparently natural question: what was the true time? Those three watches could not establish the answer at the time. The run had an actual duration, but no sufficiently precise independent record was available against which to check the hand timings. The run certainly happened; the surviving evidence of its duration consisted of those three people's button presses. Later, more precise equipment could expose the limits of such records, but it could not recover an independent timing of that particular race. The readings differed because human reactions varied and watches had errors, differences that could not be eliminated at the scale of a tenth of a second.

Then the ledger needed one number.

A procedure therefore appeared: take the median, or let the minority yield to the majority. It did not discover the true time; that was beyond its power. It produced from three candidates a result that could be written down. Once entered, that number became the time of the race. The other two disappeared.

Not being selected did not establish that they were wrong. The procedure itself did not prove those two readings inferior to the accepted one. They had first of all lost a procedural decision.

Nor did winning or losing depend on the readings alone. The same watch, operated by the same person, would have lost had the other two readings that day fallen on the opposite side. A number entered the ledger not because it was closer to something, but because it stood on the majority side that day. This is familiar elsewhere. What is striking is its occurrence in an activity widely regarded as pure measurement.

Behind every number in a record table, then, stood discarded readings at the moment of inscription. They had the same observational standing as the accepted figure. The only difference was that the ledger had one cell.

Another point matters. The three-timekeeper requirement did not appear in the general rules. It was championship practice. Once competitions began producing records, a layer of operations specifically serving records grew on top of the existing competition procedures. It was practised before it was written into the rules. Once again, the construct's sequence was practice first, text afterward.

Look again at the singular. The general rules prescribed one timekeeper, and this was no oversight. For a race that needed only to assign places, one was perfectly adequate. Three timekeepers served the record, not the race. From this moment, one competition served two constructs with different demands on the same event. One wanted to know who arrived first; the other wanted to know how long it took. The second needed three times the personnel of the first.

Majority decision itself deserves another thought. It borrowed a method from courts and deliberative bodies, originally used to settle disagreements of opinion rather than measurement. Transferring it to measurement acknowledged that at this precision, measurements occupied the same position as opinions: both required an adjudicative procedure before they could converge on one outcome. This was no one's oversight, and an age of mechanical stopwatches had no other solution. The important thing is that, once installed, the procedure no longer distinguished between rejecting an erroneous observation and rejecting one that was merely in the minority.

4. Twelve inches and eighteen inches

The association rules reproduced by Shearman also prescribed where to measure a track: twelve inches from the inner edge.

This was a very concrete act of standardization. The length of a bend depends on the line followed while measuring. The farther from the inner edge, the longer the measured circuit. Prescribing the measurement line meant prescribing how long the track was.

A note in a later annual explains that earlier records around bends had often been measured eighteen inches from the inside. The standard was subsequently changed to twelve inches, materially affecting the comparability of performances.

Measuring at eighteen inches adds a little distance relative to measuring at twelve. Thus a circuit certified by the eighteen-inch convention was actually somewhat shorter than one certified by the twelve-inch convention. Two runners completing the same number of laps, on opposite sides of this change in standards, covered different effective distances while the ledger gave their event the same name.

The appearance of this explanation in an annual shows that contemporaries knew about it. It was not treated as a scandal, nor did it prompt a clearing of the ledger. It was simply a note.

That response conveys information. If a system believed comparability to be its entire purpose, discovering two measurement conventions in its accounts ought to have caused a crisis. Recording it as a note suggests that the system's meaning did not lie entirely in comparability, or that expectations of comparability had limits from the start. Today's reader may think those people insufficiently exacting. More accurately, they were exacting about different things.

The track-surface issue has the same shape. There was no universal requirement to race only on cinders. Grass remained legal, and in discussing performances Shearman directly addressed how grass, gradients, and poor-quality cinder tracks made times hard to compare.

Before the term “world record” was formally used, then, those responsible already knew clearly that the numbers were not fully comparable. They placed them together anyway.

Let us make this more explicit. Comparability has never been a yes-or-no matter. It is a matter of degree. Every record system must stop at some level and declare that the remaining differences will be disregarded. The stopping point is determined by contemporary technical conditions and acceptable costs, not by principle alone.

A slippery inference must be avoided. Acknowledging that tolerance depends on cost does not mean the system is arbitrary or hypocritical. Every measurement stops somewhere. Even today's most precise apparatus stops at a decimal place and declares later digits irrelevant. The difference is where it stops. To call those who stopped at twelve inches careless and those who stop at a thousandth of a second rigorous is itself to judge by the later ruler. The difference between twelve and eighteen inches was tolerated because the cost of removing it was too high and the benefit too small. Later essays will show differences of the same kind deemed intolerable on other occasions, leading to the cancellation of an entire table. The treatments are opposite; the basis of judgment remains costs and benefits, not an abstract argument.

Wind belongs here, too. Long before any wind-speed threshold existed, wind was a common reason to reject a performance. Wilkinson used it to dismiss reports, and the association's record provisions expressly required wind to be considered. The early texts available to us do not establish the year in which an anemometer reading became a formal prerequisite for a record. That does not mean no process occurred. It means the process is not visible to us today.

5. Three items in one brief

On 24 April 1880 the Amateur Athletic Association was founded in Oxford. Those present resolved to form a new governing body. From the beginning it was conceived as an overarching authority, not a London club.

Earlier, the Amateur Athletic Club, founded in 1866, had stated its purpose very plainly in its constitution: to provide a ground for amateur athletics where gentleman amateurs could compete without being compelled to mix with professional runners.

The weight of that sentence belongs to the next essay. Here we need only observe that the institutions taking control of records did not inherit professional running's practices unchanged. They installed those practices inside another framework, whose first business was deciding who might enter.

The international impetus came from Sweden. In 1910–11 the Swedes had already proposed an international athletics congress. Their invitation of May 1911 specified three tasks: establish universally accepted international rules; register all records through a central body; and define amateur status for international competition.

All three appeared in the same invitation.

This fact will recur, so we should mark it now. The construct of measurement and the construct of eligibility did not emerge one after the other. They were two lines in the same brief. To establish performances comparable across countries, one had simultaneously to decide whose performances could enter the comparison. Otherwise the register would not know whom to admit. The second and third tasks required one another.

The reverse holds as well. A definition of amateur status has no means of enforcement unless attached to something that can be registered. Eligibility checks work precisely because failing them keeps a performance out of the book. The two constructs supplied each other's enforcement power, a relationship already established when they appeared together in the invitation. Later essays will examine how they operated together and whom they jointly kept outside.

On 17 July 1912, after the athletics events had ended, the congress met in Stockholm, attended by representatives from seventeen countries. One formulation of its task was to establish international athletics rules, register all world, Olympic, and national records, and define amateur status, while respecting the jurisdiction of the International Olympic Committee.

Notice the final qualification. Authority over records was conceived from the outset as existing alongside Olympic authority, not above it. This system did not grow from one centre.

The same materials record something else. Stockholm's organizers were accused of favouring Swedish interests through their event programme and rules, especially special arrangements in certain throwing events and the combined events. The allegation is explicitly documented; its existence as an allegation is certain. The organizers' response is documented too: they denied that the results actually favoured Sweden, while acknowledging that future standardization would be desirable to avoid unnecessary disputes.

Three layers must be separated. That the allegation was made is established. That the organizers responded is established. Whether the allegation was justified cannot be adjudicated from the materials now available; it remains unresolved. A response is not a refutation, and a refutation is not a fact.

Yet one thing is clear without settling the merits: the argument produced more standardization. Whether the accusation was valid or not, both sides agreed that uniform rules should prevent the next dispute. This is a characteristic way for a construct to grow. It expands not by proving itself right, but through an argument that cannot be settled. The dispute reaches no conclusion; the rules nonetheless acquire another layer.

One consequence deserves recording. Because rules grow from disputes, they cover the ground already fought over and remain silent about ground no one has contested. Silence does not mean nothing happens there. It means that what happens there has not yet made either side feel disadvantaged. The event in Essay 08 will grow in just such a silence.

6. What the sentence does not say

The materials for the Berlin meeting of 1913 contain a more developed constitutional text. Under the federation's objects appears this sentence:

To consider and register world amateur records in track and field athletics.

This is the earliest currently accessible wording that places authority over records in a constitution. It turns a convention into a jurisdiction. Before that sentence, who certified records was a matter of accepted practice. Afterward, an institution declared: this is my business.

“Consider” deserves a look. It means that a submitted performance must undergo judgment rather than taking effect automatically. Judgment needs standards, set out in other provisions. But singling out the act of judgment shows that difficult applications were already anticipated. At its foundation, an institution reserved the right to say no, placing that right before any specific criterion.

Now look at what the sentence does not contain.

It does not say that records are temporary. It does not say that the point of a record is to await being broken. It does not say that a record automatically loses its status when surpassed. It says only consider and register.

Nor do the accessible texts from 1913–14 contain a clearly promulgated provision for withdrawing an already registered record. This does not prove that none existed. It marks the limit of the available material. The question must remain open.

What is available, however, is enough to reveal a shape. The construct received the power to write entries in. It was instructed to consider and to register. About crossing entries out, the text was silent.

Something quite remarkable follows. The most widely known property of a record is that it may someday be broken. Everyone understands this; newspapers report it every year; athletes pursue it throughout their lives. Yet it does not appear in the authorizing clause examined here. It lived in practice, habit, and people's expectations; that clause explicitly conferred only the powers to consider and register.

The construct did not announce closure and non-closure together. It announced only closure. Non-closure belonged to the part left unsaid, and that unsaid part continued to operate, more powerfully even than the part expressed.

There is a counterintuitive point here. Ordinarily, absence from the rules suggests weakness. Here the reverse is true. That records will be broken requires no legislation because no one disagrees or challenges it. What needs legislation is what someone disputes. The clauses therefore do not contain the whole construct, or even its most secure parts. They record the places where it has encountered resistance.

This will return much later. When someone proposes invalidating a whole group of records at once, an unavoidable question is who has the right to cross them out. The authorizing text grants registration power. Whether that includes cancellation power requires a separate argument; the answer cannot simply be read from the original words. A ledger taught only addition is later asked to subtract.

The asymmetry between the capacities has another layer. To add a record is to prove that something happened. Evidence is present at the venue, with the timekeepers, on the measuring tape. To remove a record is to prove that something did not happen as the ledger says, when the scene has long disappeared, those involved may no longer be alive, and little remains to re-examine. The two tasks were unequal in difficulty from the beginning. That inequality has nothing to do with who holds power. It comes from the direction of time.

7. The first table reaches backward

At the Lyon congress of June 1914, the international federation proposed and adopted its first technical rules and its first world-record list. The annual printed the list under a heading specifying that these were the world records accepted by the federation during those days.

The list covered fifty-three track events, thirty race-walking events, and twelve field events. All were men's events.

Thirty race-walking events may surprise today's reader. The figure accurately reveals how different the centre of attention was then.

It reveals something else, too. The number of events in a record table is determined not by how many ways a sport can be played, but by how many variants deserve separate accounts. Creating an event promises long-term maintenance of a column, recognition of its marks, and processing of its applications. Thirty columns for race walking meant that enough people competed in those events and enough spectators watched. An event list records the distribution of attention. Attention moves, but columns may take a long time to follow. The fact that every event was for men belongs to Essay 04; we mark it here only in passing.

Now comes the essay's second central point.

The table was not principally composed of performances produced under the new rules. It reached extensively backward, recognizing older marks from the previous twenty years. It included a 220-yard performance from 1896, a mile from 1895, several long-distance performances from 1903–04, an 880-yard time from 1912, and a 440-yard time from 1913.

After writing its own rules, in other words, an institution's first act was to recognize a substantial body of performances not achieved under them.

This has the same shape as Hippias's act in the first essay. Hippias arranged names scattered across four centuries into a continuous line, which was then used as time itself. The international federation arranged performances scattered across twenty years into a table, which was then used as the world-record list. Both constructs began with retrospective recognition, supplying themselves with a past in an era when they had not existed.

An inevitable consequence followed. The recognized marks had been achieved under different measurement conventions, at different venues, with different timing arrangements. The twelve-inch and eighteen-inch standards discussed in Section 4 fall within this span. On its birthday, the first world-record table was already internally uneven.

This is not grounds for blame. The alternative was to wipe out everything before 1914 and begin from zero. That would have erased achievements everyone already recognized and left the new table empty during its early years. No one would have accepted it. Retrospective recognition was the only workable beginning. Workable does not mean clean.

One further cost deserves mention. Once admitted, those performances would be treated according to the new table's rules, although they had not been subject to those rules when achieved. Recognition simultaneously delivered them to later standards of judgment. At the time this posed no problem because no one intended to investigate backward. Much later it would, because someone always wants to investigate backward. Half the trouble in the dispute discussed in Essay 21 comes from a table that contained entries from different sources from its very beginning.

Something else appeared in the same list. Imperial and metric events were listed separately. Running had one table of distances in yards and a separate table of metric distances, each with its own holders and dates.

Conversion was therefore not accepted. A mile performance did not become a 1,500-metre record through arithmetic, nor vice versa.

In its first worldwide list, a newly created international institution retained two systems of measurement that could not be converted into one another as records. There are two valid readings. One says that this supposedly universal measurement was not universal at birth: it contained two parallel accounts. The other says that this was precisely its honesty, because the mile and 1,500 metres are different events; forced conversion would be falsification.

These readings are not rivals, one right and the other wrong. They describe two sides of the same thing, a two-sidedness that will recur throughout this series.

Before this, there were still more parallel accounts. The 1913 annual printed world, Canadian, and American records under the same event. Three names stood side by side in the 880-yard entry. The federation's table therefore did less to invent records than to announce, in a world already crowded with record tables, that one of them was the table.

8. The ledger knows only addition

Bringing these materials together reveals a clear sequence.

The need for verifiable performances first appeared in commerce and the press, among people needing a number with which to settle accounts. Clubs and associations turned dispersed verification into rules: the number of timekeepers, the measurement line, permissible starts, and which competitions could produce recognized performances. Only when international competition generated disputes that could not be settled within one country did a worldwide registry become necessary.

These three layers cannot replace one another or be compressed into one cause. Saying that records grew spontaneously out of sport and saying that gambling invented them are two versions of the same mistake. Both use one cause to explain something assembled layer by layer.

Each layer left its own remainders.

The newspaper layer left every performance that particular paper had not recorded. Selecting one authority as the standard also meant not selecting the others.

The club layer left performances achieved outside public competition, outside meetings organized by recognized clubs, or over non-prescribed distances. Those performances did happen. People were present; watches were running. Their occasions simply fell outside the register's permitted range.

The timing layer left discarded readings. These are the clearest remainders because they are exactly the same kind of thing as the accepted number. The only difference is that the ledger has one cell.

These layers share another feature. None consists of something the construct opposed. Performances absent from the newspaper; marks achieved outside recognized club meetings; the two discarded readings; marks entered as national records: none had been judged fraudulent or false. All were real, and most were acknowledged at the time. They merely fell outside this cell. What a construct cannot clear away is rarely what it wants to eliminate.

The layer of retrospective recognition left the marks that were not recognized. Before Lemming threw 62.32 metres in September 1912, he had recorded nine earlier performances recognized as Swedish records but absent from the international book. They were not false. They were registered at another level.

Another set of remainders belongs to the construct itself. It required every performance to have witnesses, measurement, signatures, and evidence open to rechecking. Yet the publicly accessible material today contains neither original record-application forms from the 1910s nor a complete list of the documents an application required. We do not know what the earliest application looked like. An institution whose central duty was preserving evidence did not preserve its own first evidence for us. This must remain unresolved, not filled in by conjecture.

The point carries a further reminder. Our view of this history is assembled from annuals, handbooks, meeting papers, and later reconstructions. Each survived for its own reasons; none was preserved to give posterity a complete picture. The history of how a registration system was established was not itself completely registered. That does not invalidate established conclusions, but it sets limits on how far they extend.

One final matter sits between this essay and the next.

The first decathlon world record recognized by the international federation was not confirmed until 1922, using an already compiled scoring table. Under that table, Thorpe's 1912 total would not be exceeded until 1926. For more than a decade, then, the highest number was not the record. What stood between those two statements was not performance, but an institution.

What happened to the man himself belongs to the next essay.

The construct received the authority to consider and register in 1913. In 1914 its first use of that authority was to write in a past over which it had exercised no jurisdiction. It learned addition. It had not been taught subtraction. Only much later would that become a problem.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.
