Before a result can qualify, a person must

Record rules appear to govern performances, but they first govern performers. The old amateur regime asked whether an entrant had ever accepted money, competed against professionals, or violated definitions shaped by class hierarchy. A superb mark made by the wrong kind of person could remain outside the book.

These definitions were often justified by an invented ancestry. Victorian administrators projected their ideal of the gentleman amateur back onto ancient Greece, even though ancient victors could receive substantial civic rewards and participate in highly organized circuits. The historical story was weak, but the rule's effect was real. A construct can enforce a false genealogy for decades; scholarly refutation and institutional repeal follow different timetables.

Jim Thorpe and the thirty-day line

Jim Thorpe won the pentathlon and decathlon at Stockholm in 1912. Months later, reports that he had been paid to play minor-league baseball triggered his disqualification. Stockholm's rules included a thirty-day period for written protests after the award ceremony, and the public disclosure arrived well beyond it.

That fact is important but not magical. Its legal force depended on whether the bodies handling the case understood themselves to be deciding a late protest or a broader eligibility question. Institutions often control a procedural safeguard by classifying the action to which it applies. Rename the matter and the deadline may disappear.

Thorpe had used his own name while other college players commonly appeared under aliases. The contrast exposes an unavoidable bias in documentary enforcement. A rule can act only on conduct it can see. The athlete who leaves an honest paper trail may be easier to punish than the athlete who conceals the same violation. No malicious official is required; visibility itself distributes risk.

Thorpe's identity as a Sac and Fox athlete educated at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School also makes a purely mechanical account inadequate. The surviving record does not supply a single document saying that race caused the sanction. It does supply a regime shaped by elite assumptions, selective visibility, and an assimilationist setting. The responsible conclusion is layered: the amateur rule existed and applied; the timing and selectivity remain open to criticism; and an Indigenous star may have received less institutional indulgence than others. None of those propositions cancels the rest.

An elastic doctrine closes around itself

Paavo Nurmi's suspension before the 1932 Olympics shows that Thorpe's treatment was not unique in type. Enforcement of amateurism could be procedurally defensible and politically contested at once. Thorpe lost achievements already made; Nurmi lost a competition that never happened, a counterfactual that no ledger could measure.

As money and international sport grew inseparable, the doctrine changed. By the early 1980s, athletics effectively defined an amateur as someone complying with its eligibility rules. The definition solved a governance problem while making the principle circular: the rules no longer had to answer to an independent meaning of amateurism. Controlled funds and compensation mechanisms then absorbed payments before professional status was openly acknowledged.

Correction by addition

In 1982 the IOC restored Thorpe as a co-champion and in 1983 presented commemorative medals to his family. Co-championship was an ingenious administrative category. It returned Thorpe without subtracting the men elevated after his disqualification or unsettling seventy years of national and statistical records.

Yet the solution repaired the book better than the event. Thorpe had not tied in 1912. Co-champion status was a later construct invented because addition was easier than deletion.

In 2022 the IOC finally listed Thorpe as the sole gold medallist in both events. Support from the families and Olympic bodies associated with the previously elevated athletes removed the final resistance. The ledger did not suddenly acquire a general power to reverse itself; people outside its original procedure created a moment in which subtraction became possible.

For years the best decathlon total belonged to a man absent from the official place he had earned. The number survived while the name was removed. When the name returned, the doctrine that had expelled him had already dissolved. Rules measure before they are fully justified, and their human costs usually mature faster than their corrections.

In this essay
  1. 1. Four gates in one definition
  2. 2. After one sentence is deleted
  3. 3. An ancestor who never existed

  5. 5. He used his own name
  6. 6. An amateur is someone who obeys the rules

1. Four gates in one definition

In 1866 the Amateur Athletic Club defined the amateur in its constitution. In the widely circulated wording of the time, he was a gentleman who had never competed in an open competition, competed for public money or admission receipts, or at any period of his life taught, pursued, or assisted athletic exercises as a means of livelihood; nor had he been a mechanic, artisan, or labourer.

There are four gates in that sentence.

The first three concern what a person has done: what kinds of competitions he entered, what money he received, how he earned his living. The fourth is different. It concerns what kind of person he is. Mechanic, artisan, labourer: none of these occupational identities has anything to do with sport. Under this sentence, a carpenter who had never received a penny for competing could not enter.

Placed in one sentence, the four gates read like aspects of a single matter. In fact they belong to two categories. The first three govern conduct, which can be investigated through witnesses and accounts. The fourth governs identity, requiring no such investigation: it is written into everyday life, known to one's neighbours. The definition thus uses two entirely different modes of judgment at once. One requires evidence; the other merely requires recognizing a person. They stand side by side, connected by a semicolon.

Another phrase deserves separate attention: “at any period of his life.”

This is no provision about present status. It reaches backward over an entire life. Someone who taught boxing for a few months at twenty because he needed to eat would still not be an amateur at forty, and never could be. This gate offered no exit, rehabilitation period, or expiry of any kind.

There was no symmetrical provision for the professional. It was explicit that a professional runner could not become an amateur again by going unpaid for several years. In the other direction, the system offered no comparable route of restoration alongside the conditions that permanently removed amateur status. The construct provided a one-way gate: once inside, you could be expelled; once outside, you could not return. Passage between categories ran one way, and a category bounded in this fashion could only contract over time.

Together, these features reveal the construct's shape. Its object of judgment was a person, not a race, and not the person as he presently stood, but his entire biography up to that moment. Before measurement began, before the ruler was taken out, this procedure was already complete.

The previous essay showed that the record construct's first ledger was a newspaper, and that the first operation it learned was addition. This essay concerns another register, placed before that ledger. A performance must be run before it can enter the record table, and this definition decided who might take the start. The division of labour was established from the outset: the later book recorded numbers; the earlier book recorded people.

2. After one sentence is deleted

The Amateur Athletic Association was founded in 1880. According to World Athletics's own historical account, the words excluding mechanics, artisans, and labourers were removed from the amateur definition at its foundation.

This must be taken seriously, because it blocks an easy narrative.

Had amateurism been nothing but a class barrier throughout, it would not have deleted its most blatant sentence only fourteen years after creating it. The deletion was real, early, and made precisely as the sport's governing institution expanded its reach.

That expansion may itself have been the reason. A club governs its members; an association governs competitions throughout a country. A national institution excluding three occupations wholesale would govern not national athletics, but the athletics of one portion of the nation. The effects would immediately appear in entry numbers and the reach of its competitions. The deletion admits many moral interpretations, but one governing logic: an institution seeking to govern the whole country cannot recognize only a small part of its people.

What remained? An encyclopedia published in 1911 recorded the association's definition in these terms: an amateur was someone who had never competed for a money prize or stake, competed with or against professionals for any prize, or taught, pursued, or assisted athletic exercises as a means of livelihood.

The occupational-identity restriction had disappeared. The prohibition on remuneration remained. Between them was a clause requiring close attention: never having competed with or against professionals.

This did not say that the person had taken money. It said that he had run alongside someone who had.

This is a logic of contagion. Eligibility can be lost through contact, without the person having committed the underlying act himself. Someone happens to share a rural race with a professional runner. He has received no money, taught no lessons, and earned no living from sport, yet his amateur standing is compromised. What the construct protects here is not the individual's innocence but the category's purity.

The gate's nature had therefore not changed. Its basis of judgment had shifted from who you were to whom you stood beside.

One practical consequence deserves separate notice. Determining who you were cost very little; it was visible at a glance. Determining whom you had stood beside cost much more. It required past competition records and knowledge of other entrants' status, information that might not survive. The new standard was fairer in wording but more dependent on archives in application. Something decisive followed: discoverability became more important than the older question of whether you belonged to a particular social type. This line runs directly to Thorpe.

Both directions of the argument must now be laid out, because both have evidence.

On one side, class exclusion lay at the core. The 1866 definition expressly named three occupations. Scholarship has described Victorian amateurism as an ideology of control and exclusion, noting that its rise coincided with growing working-class participation. Rowing had parallel exclusions. Cricket separated gentlemen and professionals in accommodation and travel. Contemporary elites did voice fears of being overwhelmed by workers. These were not incidental class overtones, but institutional designs governing entry.

On the other side, reducing the whole system to class exclusion is also a simplification. Opposition to remuneration, fair play, resistance to gambling, and hostility to overt professionalism were real components. Even scholarship arguing for the exclusionary interpretation recognizes them: the contention is that these elements were repackaged into exclusion, not that they never existed. And the 1880 deletion is a hard fact. The most nakedly exclusionary clause did not remain throughout the later system.

Neither side is the whole truth. What can be established is that the word contained both a moral claim and a social threshold from the beginning, and that the two were never separated. Anyone trying to retain only one must fight the evidence.

The cleaner claim that British amateurism simply meant people practising sport for love of it is unsupported. The earliest decisive definition was social and occupational in substance, not merely ethical or financial.

3. An ancestor who never existed

The construct found itself an origin: ancient Greece.

In 1910 a classicist published a book on Greek athletics and festivals. He wrote that athletics had become the monopoly of a class, while the old games had given way to professional exhibitions. In 1930 he published another book on athletics in the ancient world, describing excessive competition and professionalism as fatal to the true amateur spirit, and earlier athletics as purely amateur. In the same book he called corruption professionalism's greatest evil, associating late Greek and Roman athletics with spectacle, bribery, overspecialization, and the dissolution of civic competition.

These were his own formulations, not paraphrases invented by later critics.

The entire skeleton of nineteenth-century amateurism is visible in this account. There had once been a pure age; money entered; decline followed. Restoring amateur principles meant restoring that age.

In 1984 another scholar published a book specifically addressing the question, The Olympic Myth of Greek Amateur Athletics. His rebuttal had four layers.

The first was conceptual. Antiquity had no amateur ideal in the modern sense. Olympic victors regularly competed for valuable prizes, profited from athletic skill, and lacked the vocabulary and ideology required by the concept of amateurism.

He particularly emphasized the second layer: he was offering not merely an absence of evidence, but overwhelming contrary evidence and an institutional system fundamentally unable to accommodate the amateur concept. The distinction mattered because merely showing that the opposing case lacked evidence was a weaker argument.

The third layer was economic. Greek athletes competed for substantial prizes and received material rewards from their cities. This points in the same direction as Solon's reported reward schedule in the preceding essay.

The fourth was structural. Greek athletics was not organized around the amateur–professional divide at all. Those categories could not adequately describe its social reality.

Subsequent scholarship did not return to Gardiner's side. A review around 2020 compressed the field's position into a sentence: Greek athletes were neither amateurs nor professionals. This was not a compromise, but a declaration that the categories themselves had been applied in the wrong place.

In the serious literature available for examination, Gardiner's full argument has received no substantial restoration since 1984. Some narrower propositions have partly returned: early athletics could have an aristocratic character in particular contexts; crown games should not be confused with prize-money games; professionalization developed historically rather than existing in a single form from the start. These are local revisions, not rehabilitation of the overarching thesis.

The point of this section is now clear, and it is not an exposé.

A construct justified itself through a nonexistent past. Between 1866 and 1930 many people sincerely believed that past, including the classicist who wrote those sentences. He was not fabricating evidence. He was using the scholarly tools of his time to read ancient material and arriving at a conclusion suited to the needs of his age. It is easy to point out his error today, and not particularly useful.

Another matter must be put in balance. His reading worked then partly because the ancient material permits multiple readings. Crown games really did award only a wreath. Civic rewards really did arrive elsewhere. The two often appear in different passages. Someone willing to believe in ancient purity could stop after reading the first half without deliberately suppressing anything. In seeking an origin, a construct seldom needs to forge evidence. It needs only to choose suitable pieces from a body of genuine material.

What is useful is the chronology. The origin story was overturned in 1984. The construct's most blatant exclusionary clause had been removed in 1880. Its definition had been hollowed out completely in 1981. By the time scholarship finally disproved the ancestor, the rules had already dismantled themselves, for reasons unrelated to truth or falsehood.

Conversely, throughout the century in which they operated, the falsity of their basis diminished their force not for a single day. Someone disqualified under those rules lost something entirely real. Whether their origin was fictional made no difference to the person kept outside.

This will recur throughout the series, so let us state it fully. A construct's legitimating narrative and its practical force are independent. A narrative can be refuted, usually by scholars, in books. Practical force can be removed only by another construct, usually under other pressures and interests, in meeting rooms. The two follow separate timetables; neither waits for the other. When the 1984 book appeared, what it sought to dismantle had already collapsed three years earlier for different reasons.

4. Thirty days

Thorpe won the pentathlon and decathlon at Stockholm in 1912.

The official documents for those Games contained a rule that reads very specifically today: protests against an entrant's eligibility had to be made in writing and received before thirty days had expired after the award ceremony.

The first public report of Thorpe's paid baseball playing appeared in a local newspaper in January 1913, roughly six months after the Stockholm awards.

On the literal wording, the deadline had long passed.

Campaigners for restoration repeatedly invoked this point. How much work it could do remains disputed. The rule was real, the deadline was real, and the lateness was real. What is contested is whether the Amateur Athletic Union and the IOC understood themselves to be handling a formal protest under that rule. If they regarded the matter as a broader question of eligibility and awards rather than a late protest, the thirty-day provision did not govern them. We can say that the deadline supplied a powerful argument. We cannot say that contemporaries generally recognized it as conclusive.

The disagreement reveals a structure worth recording. A procedural provision can constrain an institution only if the institution acknowledges that its action is the action named by the provision. It can refuse that classification. This is not a protest, it can say, but an eligibility review; this is not a case falling under that rule, but a more general question. Change the label and the deadline falls away. The force of a procedural safeguard never lies wholly in the hands of the party it protects.

Who first exposed the baseball episode cannot now be established. We can identify the first newspaper to publish it. Later popular accounts often name a particular figure connected with baseball, but no contemporary primary document has been found that securely establishes the identification. That must remain unresolved.

The process had two stages. First the AAU revoked his amateur status. Then the IOC annulled his two championships.

Another fact matters: Thorpe himself wrote a letter admitting that he had played baseball for pay. The affair turned partly on this admission, not solely on third-party accusations.

Where is that letter today? We do not know. Where is his coach's internal correspondence? We do not know. Where is the full exchange between the AAU and IOC? Again, we do not know. What is securely identified and catalogued is his student file from the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, held by the US National Archives and Records Administration, including correspondence, financial records, and photographs.

The shape is the same as the gap in the previous essay. An institution requiring everyone to leave evidence cannot locate its own evidence at a crucial point. This time the absence is closer to a person. What survived is a school's administrative record of a student. What did not survive in an accessible location is the letter in which that person defended himself.

Deliberate destruction is unlikely. A school's student files belong to a continuing administrative system. It classifies documents and preserves them for decades because that is its daily work. A committee's one-off correspondence belongs to no continuing system. When its business is over, the group disperses; papers follow individuals into private cupboards, then disappear. Survival depends less on importance than on whether a machine is filing the documents. Important things may be easier to lose because important matters are often handled ad hoc.

One widespread account should be corrected in passing. Thorpe was not stripped of his titles on the spot in Stockholm. It happened months after the Games, in newspapers and in meetings of two committees.

5. He used his own name

A sentence in a later University of North Carolina historical account supplies the centre of this essay.

Many college athletes of the period earned money playing minor-league baseball under assumed names. Thorpe used his own. Once the facts surfaced, that made him easier to act against.

Let us follow the sentence to its end.

The rule prohibited playing for pay. Doing so under an alias violated the same rule and added deliberate concealment. Concealment might make the conduct harder to defend, yet at the stage of discovery it could have the opposite effect: an alias could shelter a player from investigation, while Thorpe, using his own name, lost two Olympic championships. This does not establish that every alias-user escaped punishment; the available material supplies no complete list.

This was not simply lax enforcement. It was how the apparatus could operate.

To process a violation, a construct must be able to see it. What it can see depends on the form in which events remain on paper. Baseball played under one's own name leaves traces in team lists, payrolls, and local newspaper reports, discoverable by anyone searching old papers. Baseball played under an alias leaves another person on those same pages. The construct did not forgive the latter. It did not know he was there.

What the apparatus can process is therefore not identical to everyone who broke the rule: it is the portion it can trace. Where identity and conduct both leave checkable records, the two can coincide. When concealment breaks the trail, violation and discoverability diverge. Someone who did not conceal the conduct may be easier to bring into the procedure precisely because that conduct is the part the apparatus can establish.

A misreading must be prevented. This does not say that the alias-users deserved punishment more, or that Thorpe deserved none. It says that an apparatus operating through visibility is statistically inclined to process the candid, and that this bias appears without anyone needing to be prejudiced. It is structural, not a question of the enforcer's character. Reducing it to unfairness in a particular enforcement action lets the deeper problem escape.

The previous essay described competitions preparing, while being staged, for their appearance on paper. Recordability was built into their physical organization. There it was a condition for entering the ledger. Here it is a condition for expulsion. The same property works in two directions.

A layer beneath that lies a single need: the construct must be able to check. Verification supplies all its authority. The newspaper chosen as standard, the three watches, and the twelve-inch measurement line all did that work. Verification can act only on what leaves traces. The more seriously the construct develops its checking apparatus, the greater, rather than smaller, its distance from what leaves none.

We now reach the part requiring particular care.

The evidence supports an interpretation concerning race, but the way it supports it must be stated precisely.

The supporting materials are these. Thorpe was a Sac and Fox Indigenous athlete educated at Carlisle, a school embedded in an assimilationist policy system. Later Indigenous commentary interprets amateurism as elitist and the punishment as also obscuring an Indigenous star. Amateurism's exclusionary origins in nineteenth-century class hierarchy made racialized enforcement possible when its rules were applied to an Indigenous athlete.

Among the accessible materials, however, no original AAU or IOC text has been found explicitly saying that he should be punished because he was Indigenous. The argument for race as a direct cause rests chiefly on institutional context, questions of selective enforcement, and later interpretive research, not on a discovered ruling explicitly expressing racism.

The two readings thus have different evidentiary forms. Mechanical application of the rule has a provision, facts, and an admission. Race as a direct cause has context, structure, and later analysis, but not that document.

A model in which both can coexist is possible, though it is not a finding. It consists of three statements: the rule existed and did apply to paid baseball; the timing and selectivity of enforcement can be questioned; an Indigenous star within assimilationist policies and an exclusionary system may not have received the discretion, leniency, or procedural shelter sometimes available to others.

All three can be true together. Their compatibility does not itself prove any one of them.

Two single-cause explanations must be avoided. The available material establishes neither racial discrimination as the sole cause of this punishment nor the neutrality of its enforcement. A racialized pattern can be argued from institutional context and selective enforcement without an explicitly racist ruling; the argument in this case must still remain proportionate to the evidence. An account based on applying the rule must likewise confront the difference an alias could make to whether a violation was discovered.

One further matter must remain unresolved. Who were those players using aliases, and how many were there? There is no complete list today. Not because no one has searched, but because by definition they were the people who left no identifiable trace. The comparison group can never be fully visible. Every estimate of the extent of selective enforcement lacks a denominator. That limits how far judgment can go. Admitting the limit is more honest than supplying a stronger-sounding conclusion.

6. An amateur is someone who obeys the rules

In April 1932 the international federation suspended Nurmi for breaches of the amateur regulations. He was subsequently excluded from the Los Angeles Olympics. The federation's Swedish leader presided over the matter.

This case serves two purposes here.

First, it shows that Thorpe's experience was not unique in kind. Penalties involving amateur status were routine during those decades, and their targets included the most famous athletes.

Second, and more importantly, Nurmi's suspension remains contested in interpretation. Finnish accounts and later nationalist narratives have often described something close to Swedish-led retaliation. Other research, including Finnish commemorative accounts, argues that the deeper issue was the federation tightening its defence against encroaching professionalism.

The disagreement matters less for choosing a winner than for what it reveals generally: enforcement of amateur rules could be defensible in their wording and contested politically at the same time. A rule can be properly applied and still raise a reasonable question about why it was applied on this occasion. The two are not mutually exclusive.

Nurmi's case also differs from Thorpe's in a revealing way. Thorpe was dealt with retrospectively, after achieving his results; something already made was taken away. Nurmi was stopped beforehand; what was removed had not yet happened. The first loss can be measured: the two championships are identifiable. The second cannot, because no one knows what he would have run in Los Angeles. The construct's action had the same form in both cases. One remainder had a shape; the other never acquired one.

Then came the fate of the word itself.

In 1976 the international federation still used an older conception of amateurism linked to sporting spirit, while already permitting national associations to compensate lost earnings and limited travel expenses.

In 1981 the congress changed the definition. An amateur now meant someone who complied with the federation's eligibility rules.

Pause over that sentence.

Before it, “amateur” was a word with substantive content. That content might come from ancient Greece, a moral position, or a class's way of life. Wherever it came from, it came from outside the organization. Precisely because it was external, one could use it to question the organization: do your rules accord with amateur ideals?

After the sentence, that question could no longer be asked. If an amateur was someone who followed our rules, asking whether our rules accorded with amateur ideals became asking whether our rules accorded with our rules.

Closure was complete, on condition that the question could no longer be posed.

The new definition need not have been understood at the time as an act of self-authorization. It looked more like practical tidying. The old definition had diverged so far from actual practice as to become unenforceable. Rather than preserve a standard everyone evaded, why not replace it with one that could be applied? From a governing perspective, that was responsible. The important point is that responsible administration and self-closure were exactly the same act here. Constructs do not achieve closure only by exceeding their authority. They often do so by getting things into order.

In 1982 the federation formally established trust funds, allowing money to reach athletes under federation control without openly acknowledging that the sport had become professional. Scholarship has called this a soft transition from amateurism to professionalism. By the early 1990s athletics was plainly professional, although institutional language changed more slowly.

There is no agreed date on which amateur provisions disappeared completely from the federation's rules. We can establish the hollowing-out process between 1976 and 1982, and the fact of professionalism by the early 1990s. We cannot establish when the final occurrence of “amateur” was deleted from every layer of constitution and regulation. This was a plural process: definitions, compensation mechanisms, commercial expansion, and general acceptance of professionalism each had their own timetable.

The familiar account therefore needs revision. Athletics' amateur era did not end when someone first received money. Payment channels were first brought under federation management; only afterward was professionalism acknowledged. Before abandoning something, the construct took it over.

7. A solution without subtraction

In 1982 the IOC approved a restoration measure. In January 1983 commemorative medals were presented to Thorpe's family.

The measure provided replica gold medals and returned him to the records as a co-champion, not the sole winner.

By using co-champion status, it left untouched the athletes promoted after his disqualification. Norway's Bie and Sweden's Wieslander remained in place.

Here we can see the layers of resistance confronting a correction. First are the two names: neither man had done anything wrong, and taking something from them required a separate justification. Second are their national Olympic committees: the gold medals had stood in two countries' records for seventy years. Third are the records themselves: every book, register, and statistical account citing the table during those seventy years would become inaccurate. Altering an entry never affects that entry alone.

This is a particularly clear specimen, picking up precisely where the preceding essay ended.

The construct received the power to consider and register in 1913; its authorizing text was silent about deletion. Seventy years later the IOC faced exactly this problem. To put Thorpe back would require taking out two others already entered. But the ledger knew only addition.

It therefore invented a category. “Co-champion” allowed a correction to be achieved entirely through addition: add Thorpe, subtract no one. The two 1912 events now each had two champions, an outcome that had not existed in their competitive format at the time.

The solution repaired the accounts. It did not repair the event itself.

A man's performances had been annulled, and the method of restoring them was to declare him equal to the men substituted for him. The arithmetic worked; the history did not. Neither event had been tied. He won; the others lost. The category was invented to accommodate the ledger's operational limits, not the event.

Once created, however, the category became a real thing. Subsequent tables genuinely showed two champions in each event. Later readers found that result without seeing how it had arisen. A label improvised to solve the construct's technical problem remains in its accounts in precisely the same form as any other entry. After a time, original entries and patches become indistinguishable. The retrospectively assembled victor list in Essay 01 became time itself in the same way.

Fairness requires one further point. This may indeed have been the only proposal capable of passing then. Revoking the other titles involved two other national Olympic committees, seventy-year-old records, and two individuals who had themselves done nothing wrong. Addition was the path of least resistance. Often that is the only passable path.

Workable, again, does not mean clean.

8. Authorization from outside

In July 2022 the IOC announced that Thorpe would be listed as the sole gold medallist in the 1912 Stockholm pentathlon and decathlon.

One hundred and ten years.

Only one word distinguished this from 1983, but that word was everything. The earlier restoration was non-exclusive: he was a co-champion. In 2022 exclusivity returned: he was the sole champion. The 1983 act had been addition. The 2022 act did what the construct had not known how to do nearly forty years earlier.

How did subtraction become possible?

According to the IOC, an organization campaigning persistently for the change and the support of an IOC member helped move it forward. Related reports contain something more important. The Swedish Olympic Committee and Wieslander's surviving relatives confirmed that he had never accepted the gold medal and always regarded Thorpe as the sole rightful champion. The Norwegian side supplied corresponding confirmation concerning Bie.

What made subtraction possible, then, was not that the construct had developed a new power of cancellation. The people represented by those two entries said that their entries did not count.

Precision matters here. Their statements had no binding legal force, and the IOC did not act under compulsion. The confirmation removed the final resistance. Once those being displaced publicly said they had never accepted their titles, preserving the status quo lost its available justification. What the construct needed was not authorization but a moment when no one objected. Such a moment had to be awaited, until everyone concerned was willing to say the same thing. Only time could supply it.

The construct could not take them out. They walked out from within.

The shape of this event matters to the entire series. The preceding essay explained that addition and subtraction were unequal from the beginning. Evidence for addition existed at the scene; evidence for subtraction had dispersed. The inequality came from time's direction. Here there was an exception, made possible precisely because someone outside the proceeding kept remembering. Wieslander's non-acceptance of the medal stood in no official ledger. It passed through a family for a hundred and ten years, then was brought forward when needed.

In this case the original recognition procedure did not automatically produce its own correction. Reconsideration also required memories and material mobilized beyond the existing entries. That does not mean an institution cannot create internal review or revocation procedures, or that an earlier determination must stand forever. Registration is not a substitute for renewed judgment. Whether material outside the ledger can enter still depends on someone remembering, the rememberer remaining available, and a willingness to speak. All three are contingent.

Return to the original definition.

The sentence of 1866 judged a person across his whole past, with no exit or expiry. The procedure of 1913 removed a person from behind two performances, although no one claimed the performances were false. What he had run, jumped, and thrown remained. His name was extracted. The thread left dangling in the preceding essay belongs here: the first internationally recognized decathlon world record was confirmed only in 1922, while Thorpe's 1912 total under the relevant scoring table was not surpassed until 1926. For more than a decade, the highest number belonged to a man absent from the list. The number remained; the person was removed.

The gate itself later dissolved. A sentence was deleted in 1880; the substance was emptied in 1981; by the early 1990s the word no longer pointed to anything operative. When the name returned to its exclusive position in 2022, the rules he had once been accused of breaking had long disappeared.

The rest of this series will repeatedly encounter that order. A construct operates first and leaves costs behind. Recognition of those costs often comes after the construct has changed or vanished. Part of what makes recognition possible is that no one needs to defend the old rules anymore. That neither diminishes the recognition nor renders it insincere. It explains why correction comes so late: while rules are still operating, the price of admitting their error must be paid by those currently using them.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before:
Nine women finished

The women's 800 metres at the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics became one of sport's most durable cautionary tales. Lina Radke won in a world record of 2:16.8, Kinue Hitomi finished second, and all nine finalists completed the race. Contemporary retellings nevertheless described a scene of widespread collapse and used the spectacle to support the event's removal from the Olympic programme until 1960.

Later examination of film, photographs, and race accounts shows how much the story grew in transmission. World Athletics' own historical material now states that one athlete collapsed and none suffered serious harm. Exhausted runners bending or lying down after a middle-distance final were turned into evidence that the distance itself exceeded the female body.

The dispute was never simply about what happened on the track. It concerned what observers were prepared to see. Fatigue that signified heroic effort in men could signify biological unsuitability in women. A visual interpretation became a policy fact.

The decision and the missing minutes

The official process is less complete than the famous narrative. We can reconstruct the programme change and the surrounding public reaction more readily than a single decisive vote with a transparent scientific basis. The absence matters because later accounts often compress a diffuse institutional retreat into one self-evident verdict: women tried, collapsed, and were protected from themselves.

That sentence turns several contestable judgments into a natural sequence. It hides disagreements among the IOC, athletics officials, women's sport organizations, journalists, and national delegations. It also hides the political bargain through which women had received only five athletics events in 1928 in the first place.

A parallel record world

Women had not arrived in Amsterdam without athletic history. The Fédération Sportive Féminine Internationale organized competitions and recognized records outside the male-governed structures that restricted them. Radke entered the Games already holding the accepted FSFI world record. The Olympic race did not create women's middle-distance capacity; it moved a portion of an existing athletic world into another institution's field of vision.

This produces two rooms. In one, women compete, improve records, and build organizations. In the other, the dominant international system decides whether those bodies and marks will count in its own chronology. Recognition can arrive later than performance because recognition is not the same act as measurement.

Number bibs and institutional sight

An athlete becomes legible through entry lists, eligibility checks, assigned lanes, officials, and a record form. A runner outside that apparatus may cover the same distance in the same time without producing an official mark. The body's capacity is continuous; the institution's field of measurement is bordered.

Women's sport made this border unusually visible. Performances often existed before the governing system created a place for them. The later official record table could then reach backward and incorporate some results, giving the impression that the system had always been the natural home of the event.

A verdict about bodies made from a story

The 1928 episode did not reveal a physiological limit. It revealed how quickly a narrative could become a classification. Nine athletes completed the final, yet distress at the finish was made to speak for women as a category. The institution did not merely measure bodies; it decided which observations represented the body it thought it was measuring.

The eventual return of the Olympic 800 metres in 1960 did not restore thirty-two years of races that had never been staged at the Games. A later rule can reopen a door, but it cannot produce the careers and comparisons excluded while the door was shut.

The deepest loss is therefore counterfactual. We know the marks women recorded elsewhere. We cannot know the Olympic fields, rivalries, tactical innovations, or champions that the programme prevented from existing. A construct can repair its table while remaining unable to measure what its earlier table caused not to happen.

1. All nine finished

Amsterdam, 1928. The women's 800-metre final.

Nine athletes started, and all nine were listed as finishers. The first three ran faster than the pre-race world record. Radke won in 2:16.8, followed by Kinue Hitomi in 2:17.6 and Gentzel in 2:17.8. Then came Thompson, Rosenfeld, MacDonald, Dollinger, and Kilosówna.

The ninth finisher was Wever. Commonly reproduced results do not give her precise time.

We need not invest this fact with too much weight. A missing last-place time in an early results table could have many explanations: an omission in recording, a loss in copying, or a failure to time it originally. What matters is its position. In a race where three women bettered the world record, the only athlete without a number was the one who finished last. The construct's attention declines with placing, and the bottom cell is where its grip most readily loosens.

By any measure, this was a successful race. An event entered the Olympics for the first time; nine women finished; three beat the existing world record. If measurement was the construct's purpose, what happened in this final was the best result it could have hoped for.

One further point follows. Three leading athletes bettering the pre-race record in the same final shows a recorded frontier being advanced together. That record had already been improving, while participation and documentation in the event continued to expand. One final alone cannot establish how narrow the earlier field had been. The table nevertheless carried two meanings: athletes demonstrated real competitive ability, and an event was accumulating its own history. One was athletic, the other institutional. This should have been a development the construct was prepared to take seriously.

Surviving film can still be viewed. It shows several athletes briefly sitting down, lying on the grass, or visibly gasping after the finish. None of this is unusual after an 800-metre race.

The doctor examining the women afterward was Bergmann. A few minutes later she checked their pulses, blood pressure, and general condition. Her report was that everything was normal.

The evidentiary position was therefore clear from the outset: an official results table, film, and testimony from the doctor who examined the athletes on the spot. All three corroborated one another and pointed to the same conclusion. Nine women ran a fast 800 metres, then were tired.

Their different natures strengthen that corroboration. The results table was institutional, produced by procedure without evaluative commentary. The film was mechanical; it did not know what it was filming. The testimony was professional, given at the scene by someone qualified to judge. Three independent sources pointed to the same event. Evidentially, that is a fairly strong state of confirmation.

What happened next had nothing to do with those three things.

2. The newspapers said five, or six

Around 3 August 1928, several major newspapers reported the race.

The Times described the aftermath as a spectacle of prostrate figures in evident distress, inferring that the women's 800 metres was dangerous.

Williams of The New York Times wrote that the event demanded too much of women's physical powers. He also reported that six of the nine collapsed after finishing and several had to be helped away.

Shirer of the Chicago Tribune put the claim directly in his headline: five women track stars had collapsed in an Olympic race.

In Canada's Toronto Star, Marsh wrote about Thompson and Rosenfeld on the front page of 3 August, turning exhaustion into a selling point for the story.

Set these reports beside the three sources in the previous section.

The official table says nine finished. The New York Times says six fell. The Chicago Tribune says five collapsed.

These numbers do not directly cancel one another out. Nine finishers and five or six athletes lying down afterward could coexist: finishing and post-race collapse are different indicators. What needs checking is which movements were called falling or collapsing, and whether they supported the conclusion that the distance was dangerous.

We must not overstate the point. There is descriptive latitude between briefly sitting down and collapsing. The same movement can be described as resting or giving way. The numbers need not have been invented. They may have classified what was seen by a standard much looser than the results table's. The point is not that someone lied. It is that when description and counting conflicted, description took effect.

Something else needs stating, and it is the most important point in this section.

None of these four reporters can be securely placed beside the finish line at the time. Modern research can establish their bylines, newspapers, and publication dates. It cannot determine from the surviving material whether they saw the scene themselves or wrote from reports passed around the stadium. Four articles, four vantage points: all unresolved.

Nor did the present research recover directly quotable facsimiles of the original reports in leading German and French newspapers. Modern scholarship broadly agrees that the catastrophic narrative was international, not confined to Britain and North America. But establishing that directly requires national-library microfilms and facsimiles. We cannot now describe in fine detail how widely, and in exactly what language, the story circulated.

That gap has a practical effect. Seeing only four English-language reports makes it difficult to decide whether this was a few newspapers independently dramatizing the same story or a shared framework spanning languages. The former looks more like a journalistic contingency; the latter more like an age's common preconception. Scholarship favours the latter, but the direct texts supporting it were not recovered in this research. The analysis below must therefore rest on the four visible articles, not pronounce on the invisible ones.

The preceding essay's observation applies directly: what a construct can see depends on the form in which an event remains on paper.

Here the difficulty is that the same event remained on paper in two forms, each emphasizing different aspects of it.

One was a results table, produced by timekeepers, judges, and the meeting's recording procedures, whose entire function was to record accurately what had happened. The other was news, produced by pages that had to sell, whose function was to persuade readers that the story was worth reading.

The latter took effect.

This must be stated fully, because it can sound like a complaint about journalism. It is not. Essay 02 explained that the modern record system's first ledger was itself a commercial newspaper. Wilkinson selected it because it was the only archive large enough and continuous enough at the time. Newspapers had helped bring the construct into existence. The same medium gave it a body in one place and overturned its measurements in another. These are two sides of one property: whatever can bring news before everyone can also bring an erroneous number before everyone, just as quickly.

3. The vote did not survive

After Amsterdam, the international athletics federation decided to remove the women's 800 metres from the 1932 programme.

An accessible first-hand account of the rationale comes from Bergmann. She summarized it this way: delegates were disturbed by the image of the prostrate girls and voted on humanitarian grounds. She also said that the German delegates had tried to preserve the event.

The German effort deserves notice. Germany had won the title and set the new world record, giving it a direct reason to defend the event. But Japan and Sweden also won medals, and reasons to preserve an event extend beyond medals; Germany was not its only beneficiary. This neither praises nor condemns anyone. It reminds us that gains and losses may influence voting positions without allowing us to infer everyone’s motives from the identity of the champion.

A structural question follows. New events may not yet have established training resources, competitive pathways, and networks of support across many countries. When programmes contract, they may therefore find their place harder to defend than older events. This is no law governing every new event, nor does it reduce every vote to an interest calculation. It shows that, beyond an event’s intrinsic merits, the distribution of existing investment and support may help determine what survives.

Then there is the more widespread claim that the IOC immediately voted to limit women's racing distances to 200 metres.

No matching decision appears in the publicly verifiable minutes.

What can be established is another vote. In 1931 the IOC voted on women's participation in athletics overall. By sixteen votes to three, it retained women's athletics in the 1932 programme. The minutes preserve neither the debate point by point nor a directly verifiable separate vote count for the women's 800 metres.

The familiar claim must therefore remain unresolved. This does not mean it is necessarily wrong. It means the original record supporting it is not currently available.

A pattern appearing for the third time deserves marking.

In Essay 02, the earliest original record-application form could not be found. In Essay 03, the locations of Thorpe's admission letter, his coach's internal correspondence, and the complete exchange between committees were unknown. Here a decision governing thirty-two years has left no itemized record of its reasoning.

None of these three cases requires deliberate destruction. What survived shares a property: it was the routine output of a continuing machine. Annual results books were printed every year; student files were classified; aggregate vote totals entered minutes. Systems performed those tasks. What failed to survive also shares a property: it was one-off. A discussion, a letter, a debate. Once concluded, it dispersed.

A construct therefore usually leaves posterity its conclusions, not its reasoning.

The consequences for judgment are concrete. To understand what lay behind the 1928 deletion, we have a decision's result, a doctor's recollections, and later accounts. We lack what those present actually said that day. Conclusions about motives must therefore infer from outcomes and context. Inference cannot attain the certainty of meeting records. This is a limit to accept, not an obstacle to overcome by interpreting harder.

4. The reasons from within

We must now work through both directions of the argument. Here both have established evidence; neither needs to be contrived.

One direction says that removing the event rested chiefly on a mistaken assessment of women's abilities. The supporting evidence has already appeared: nine official finishers, three bettering the pre-race world record, surviving film that does not support the familiar story of multiple fainting athletes, and the examining doctor's judgment that the prohibition was hasty and emotional, with normal physiological findings. Besides Bergmann, Messerli later said he had been present and that the supposed collapse looked more like crying and emotional reactions to defeat than pathological breakdown. Taylor interpreted brief post-race falls by individual competitors as tension and competitive emotion, not proof that the distance was unbearable.

Bergmann made a more important observation: nervous strain in sprints might be more harmful than longer-distance running.

Its significance is that the medical opinion available on the spot did not point toward the decision. The doctor examined the athletes and judged in the opposite direction.

Of course, her suggestion was itself one doctor's opinion, not an established finding. Caution is necessary before using it as proof that the decision was wrong: that would counter one untested professional judgment with another. Its force lies elsewhere. It shows that medical opinion was not unified, although later accounts often portray the removal as following contemporary medical consensus. “Consensus” is inapplicable here. There was none.

The other direction says that the decision had reasons within its contemporary medical and organizational setting, and those reasons were coherent within that framework of knowledge.

That framework had roughly three layers. First, women's bodies were understood primarily as bodies for reproduction and child-rearing. Moderate exercise was beneficial, while excessive or competitive endurance exertion might harm health and fertility. Second, an unbecoming public spectacle after a race was treated as a governing problem: the concern was what spectators saw, not whether athletes were injured. Third, there was a preference for women's Olympic events described as aesthetic. IOC president Baillet-Latour's position in 1930 pointed this way.

The second layer is particularly revealing because it is independent of the athletes' physical condition. It concerns an image, precisely what the newspapers supplied.

There is another reason to isolate this point. The first layer concerns physical harm to athletes, a claim that evidence can test. The second concerns public appearance, the third a preference for aesthetic events. Those are not the same kind of bodily assertion and cannot be decided by a medical examination alone. This does not exempt impressions and preferences from criticism. It means that showing athletes can withstand the distance does not automatically remove the other two reasons. A decision may lose its bodily rationale yet persist through programme preferences. This is why accumulating evidence does not always change a decision.

These are consequently not two opposing explanations. They interlock within one event. Newspapers magnified the image; the image entered delegates' judgments; and the contemporary framework already offered a channel through which public appearance counted as a legitimate reason. None of the three alone need have produced the deletion. Together they were sufficient.

A limitation must be explicit. The present public-source research did not produce an item-by-item, edition-by-edition bibliography of medical articles and textbooks around 1928. It recovered the intellectual structure of the restrictive position and the on-site medical testimony against restriction, but not a bibliography whose individual entries could all be checked. That does not mean no such bibliography exists. It lies outside what this research recovered.

Finally, consider the difference in timing between the two directions.

Evidence later systematically weakened the mistaken assessment of ability, while the logic of programme governance persisted in the history of the rules. The latter half of this essay will show it: by 1978, the reason for rejecting women's 5,000 and 10,000 metres was no longer physical incapacity but insufficient worldwide participation. The reason changed. The gate stayed where it was.

5. Another record book

Long before Amsterdam, another system was already operating.

During the 1920s, Milliat organized independent international women's competitions to pressure the IOC and the athletics federation. The four central competitions staged by the Fédération Sportive Féminine Internationale were Paris in 1922, Gothenburg in 1926, Prague in 1930, and London in 1934.

The federation did more than hold meetings. From 1922 onward, it recognized women's world records.

That is the central fact here. Recognizing records is not ancillary to organizing competitions. Establishing, ratifying, and publishing them are among an international sport federation's core functions. Doing this declares that one is an institution entitled to say: this number counts.

Notice that no one had conferred the power on it. The FSFI did not obtain record authority from a higher body. It began doing the work, and because athletes competed, newspapers reported, and people took the numbers seriously, it acquired the function in practice. Essay 02 explained that a table needs a source whose credentials it cannot grant itself. Here is the other side: an institution can become that source by doing the work continuously.

Between 1922 and 1936, women's athletic performances therefore belonged to two books.

A compromise was reached in 1926. Milliat agreed to replace the name “Women's Olympic Games” with “Women's World Games” in exchange for women's athletics entering the 1928 Olympics. The bargain reveals her strategy. The parallel system was not intended to endure forever. It was bargaining power.

The compromise was only partly honoured. Women's athletics entered Amsterdam as a limited set of events, not a full programme. The Women's Amateur Athletic Association in Britain consequently refused to send a team: ten events had been promised, but only five were offered.

This was a rare boycott by women for programme equality in modern Olympic history. Its target was precisely the admission usually narrated as a victory.

In 1936 the FSFI was absorbed by the international athletics federation.

Absorption differed from the treatments seen in earlier essays. It neither wiped out the other ledger nor preserved two books side by side. World Athletics's present accounts of women's record progressions still state that certain earliest world records were recognized by the FSFI in 1922. Some entries from the absorbed book therefore remain within the official genealogy.

We do not, however, possess an itemized list of which entries were taken over intact and which were later silently invalidated. Public evidence establishes a transfer of authority, but cannot produce a line-by-line handover inventory.

The current book thus contains entries from an institution that no longer exists, without their origins necessarily being visible on its face. After swallowing a rival, a construct does not label which lines were swallowed.

The parallel ledger was never declared invalid while it existed. It was real, recognized by a functioning international organization, pursued by real athletes. It disappeared not because it was refuted, but because part of its purpose was achieved and its organizers had never intended it to last indefinitely. A construct can end through completion rather than defeat.

Yet that formulation must not be too tidy. What was completed was Milliat's layer of purpose. For athletes whose performances appeared in the four Women's World Games, the relevant question was not whether the ledger had fulfilled its purpose but whether their own names remained in it. We cannot fully answer that today because the itemized transfer inventory does not exist. A construct's ending is not the same event for its designers and for the people it records.

6. The woman without a number and the woman with one

The women's 800 metres returned at Rome in 1960.

From 1928 to 1960: thirty-two years.

The restoration has no single identifiable date. We know the event was on Rome's programme. Public materials do not securely pin down who completed the final act of reinstatement, in which meeting and year. More cautiously, it resulted from the continuing expansion of women's events during the 1950s and reconsideration of the programme by the athletics federation and IOC, rather than one definitive meeting of vindication.

Pause over this.

Closing the gate had concrete acts: a vote, an occasion on which reasons could be stated, a conclusion that could enter minutes. Opening it did not. The opening was dispersed across more than a decade, accumulating through incomplete individual actions until we can no longer identify the moment it was accomplished.

A construct closes and opens gates asymmetrically. Closing requires a decision because it resists the status quo. Opening may require only that the status quo gradually cease to need the gate. The latter produces no single record.

This also explains why commemoration concentrates on closure. In 1928 there is an identifiable object: a vote, reasons, quotable sentences. The reopening offers no equivalent. Later accounts therefore revolve around the moment of closure, leaving the decade or more of opening almost blank for lack of quotable milestones. The construct's method of recording determines what posterity remembers, and what it records is often precisely its worst decisions.

The later completion of the women's programme can be traced through official results: 1,500 metres at Munich in 1972; 3,000 metres and the marathon at Los Angeles in 1984; 10,000 metres at Seoul in 1988; triple jump at Atlanta in 1996; pole vault and hammer at Sydney in 2000; and the 3,000-metre steeplechase at Beijing in 2008.

From 1928 to 2008: eighty years.

Along that line sit two events close together, offering a particularly clear comparison.

In 1966 Gibb joined the Boston Marathon from bushes beside the start and ran 3:21:40. She had no race number.

In 1967 Switzer obtained a number using her initials and became the first woman to complete Boston wearing one.

The construct responded to the two women quite differently.

For Gibb, the dispute concerned the organizers' doubt that she had covered the whole course. The response was to deny that the event had happened. She was not registered, so nothing could be cancelled. All that remained was to challenge whether the performance was valid, a challenge not readily resolved within the system because she had never been part of its timing and check-in procedures.

For Switzer, the response was a physical attempt to remove her from the course. She wore a number, appeared in the register, and was an identifiable entry.

The Thorpe pattern repeats. The person using his own name was processed; the aliases escaped. Here it is more direct: the registered person could be seized. The construct could do little to the unregistered person, and precisely for that reason could say she had not finished.

The two responses carried different costs. The attempt to seize Switzer produced a sequence of photographs. Those images became the incident's best-known evidence and worked strongly against the organizers. Doubt about Gibb left no such images, because doubt was a statement, not a physical act. When the construct acted on a visible entry, its own action became visible. When it dealt with an invisible person, its action remained invisible too. Visibility runs both ways, something it may not have anticipated.

A formal women's division was established in 1972. The organizers later recognized Gibb's pioneering-era victories.

7. Records first, admission afterward

In 1978 the international federation's women's committee requested world-record recognition and international competition status for the 5,000 and 10,000 metres.

The federation refused, saying worldwide participation had not reached a sufficiently high level.

In 1980 it recognized world records in both, but still did not include them in its then-existing world-championship and international-competition programme. Under the rule governing new Olympic events, they consequently could not make the 1984 Los Angeles programme.

Two things must be separated.

First is the sequence. Records came first; programme eligibility followed. For several years there were officially recognized world records in events that the recognizing institution did not admit to its major competitions. Measurement was operating before the gate of admission opened.

Essay 03 showed the reverse sequence: first draw the eligibility line, then measure those who crossed it. Here measurement came first, and admission only much later. They were the same two books in reversed order. Either way, some people remained caught between them.

Second is the reason itself.

Insufficient participation has a structural problem as a ground for refusal: an event's worldwide participation depends heavily on Olympic status. Without an Olympic event, countries do not allocate national-team places or training resources to it; young athletes do not choose that path. Participation remains low, and the threshold stays unmet.

The gate requires applicants to possess something obtainable only by passing through the gate.

This need not be a deliberately designed trap. Any institution controlling its own size needs a standard for what deserves inclusion. Popularity is among the most neutral and readily measurable standards available. The difficulty lies not in its intention but in its mathematical form: it makes an outcome into a prerequisite.

Such forms occur elsewhere. A technology needs widespread adoption to become cheap, and needs to become cheap to be widely adopted. A language needs users to be worth learning, and learners to acquire users. The difference is that those situations do not ordinarily place a switch in one institution's hands. This one does. When a loop contains an institution able to authorize an exception, it is no longer only a natural delay. It is also a choice that could have been made and was not. That matters in judgment without imputing malice to anyone.

In 1984 several women distance runners sued in California, asking the appellate court to require the addition of women's 5,000 and 10,000 metres to that year's Los Angeles Olympics. They argued that the IOC's new-event rule historically locked women into an inferior position and perpetuated structural discrimination against female athletes.

The Ninth Circuit upheld the refusal of a preliminary injunction. The majority held that the rule applied on its face equally to men and women, and therefore was not the kind of legal sex classification it understood to be at issue.

Allegations and judgment must be read separately.

The dissent expressly acknowledged that the early modern Olympics were marred by blatant discrimination against women, and argued for applying California's anti-discrimination law more favourably to the plaintiffs.

The case therefore did not find that the IOC had never discriminated. The majority found that, within this lawsuit's particular structure, the current rule did not justify immediately compelling additional events by judicial order. These are entirely different propositions, often collapsed in later retellings.

The majority's reasoning itself illustrates a recurring form in this series. A rule treats everyone equally in wording, but acts on a status quo made by an unequal history. It inherits the existing distribution and treats it neutrally. The neutrality is not necessarily a disguise; it is genuine. The important point is that neutrality toward an asymmetric starting point does not produce a symmetric result.

The majority must also be allowed its own place. The court faced not the general question of whether the rule was fair, but whether it could immediately order an international organization to add two events in this litigation. The answers may differ. Restricting itself to the second question was not necessarily evasion. The dissent addressed history; the majority addressed what this judicial intervention could accomplish. They were not discussing precisely the same thing, and their coexistence is no contradiction.

Whether the situation amounted to discrimination in law is another question, to which the 1984 majority and dissent gave different answers.

8. Two rooms

The gate closed in 1928 is open today.

The Paris Olympics achieved gender parity in athlete quota places. The IOC's own event totals were 157 men's events, 152 women's events, and twenty mixed events.

In athletics, the remaining asymmetry is chiefly no longer that women lack an event, but that corresponding events take different forms. Men run the 110-metre hurdles; women run the 100-metre hurdles, with different spacings and heights. Men's combined competition is the decathlon; women's is the heptathlon.

That change is one of the essay's most important points: exclusion on grounds of capacity has become differentiation through rules.

The rationale in 1928 was that women could not withstand the distance. Today's rationale invokes historical tradition, competitive comparability, and continuity of rules. The first makes a bodily claim that evidence can refute, and has refuted. The second cannot be refuted in that way because it makes no bodily claim. It says only that these events have always had these forms, and changing them would make earlier and later results incomparable.

This transition deserves fair treatment. Replacing a false assertion about bodies with a true assertion about continuity in the accounts is progress in every sense, forced by decades of evidence. The construct abandoned an untenable reason for a defensible one. What must remain visible is that the gate's position largely stayed fixed while its inscription changed. A construct can change its grounds without changing its shape, and criticism itself often drives the change of grounds.

And the continuity claim is true.

Decathlon and heptathlon are two event sets, two scoring tables, and two record lists. Their performances cannot be converted into one another. This is design, not oversight. To preserve comparisons across time within each, incomparability between them must be maintained indefinitely.

The structure will recur after Essay 05, but appears here with unusual clarity. The two ledgers run in parallel not because one defeated the other or one was invalidated, but because comparability can be achieved only within a ledger. Extending one column of numbers requires refusing to merge it with another. Each ledger purchases its internal integrity through incommensurability with the others.

Here the essay reconnects with Essay 01. The ancient victor list produced names rather than comparability, so four tracks of different lengths posed no problem. The later construct chose comparability. Once that became its purpose, it had continually to draw boundaries: which performances could stand together and which could not. Every boundary left something outside. Across eighty years, the grounds shifted from bodies to participation, then to tradition and continuity. The number of boundaries did not diminish.

Return to that afternoon in 1928.

Nine women finished a fast 800 metres. The results table recorded nine names and eight times; the ninth finisher Wever's time does not appear in common compilations. Film survived; the examining doctor left testimony. Neither determined what happened afterward.

What took effect was a handful of newspaper stories. Whether their authors stood at the finish line cannot now be established.

The construct possessed its own measurements. Its entire apparatus existed to produce the results table: timekeepers, judges, recording procedures. Then it looked at the athletes on the grass and set its own measurements aside.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.after: 那一天到场的不止比蒙一个人，还有四个需要一起考虑的因素：海拔、风、一条新跑道，以及运动员本人的状态。它们共同参与了那一跳，而事后留下的资料不足以把各自的贡献干净地分开。同届比赛还采用了新的计时装置；它改变的是短跑成绩的记录，不是跳远的物理距离。后面会看到，这两类问题怎样被同一个制度处理。
edits.reason: 原1.8计时被列为影响那一跳的第四变量，4.7却为运动员状态，6.12又明确计时与跳远无关。必须明确两层；不删计时线索，也不把它当跳远因果变量。

edits.after: 所以这一篇不打算给墨西哥城帮了比蒙多少一个确定的数值。现存证据还不足以让这个问题得到不依赖具体模型的精确答案。这一篇追问的是，为什么答案仍然带着条件，以及一个以精确度量为业的构，遇到一件尚不能充分归因的事情时，会怎么办。
edits.reason: 保留归因未决主旨，把无答案的绝对断言限到现存证据与精确分配，避免与后文模型工作矛盾。
